Ms Lim invests S$100,000 in a 5-year equity-linked note. A zero-coupon bond returns her principal at maturity and a call option provides market participation. The reference stock falls 40% over the term. The product issuer has not provided a separate guarantee. Which statement about Ms Lim's position at maturity is most accurate?

options.A: She loses 40% of her capital because the note mirrors the stock one-for-one
options.B: Her capital is at risk only if the zero-coupon bond issuer defaults, not merely because the reference stock fell
options.C: She receives the full market gain because the stock fall makes the call option more valuable
options.D: The note guarantees S$100,000 regardless of any issuer's creditworthiness

questions.explanation: The zero-coupon bond returns principal at maturity if its issuer does not default. The call option simply expires worthless when the stock falls, producing no participation payoff. Capital risk arises from the bond issuer's credit, not from the reference stock's price move. The product provides downside protection through the bond component, not an unconditional guarantee.

questions.stem: An adviser must choose between wrapping a client's structured investment as a structured deposit or a structured fund (unit trust). Which distinction is most significant for the client's protection if the issuing institution fails?

options.A: A structured deposit ranks ahead of a fund unit in liquidation because deposits always receive priority
options.B: A structured deposit is covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme, unlike a structured fund
options.C: A structured fund holds assets through an independent trustee, so the client has beneficial ownership separate from the issuer's balance sheet; a structured deposit holder is an unsecured creditor of the bank
options.D: Both wrappers give identical creditor protection because MAS regulates both

questions.explanation: A structured fund (CIS) holds assets through a third-party trustee, so investors have beneficial ownership that is not part of the issuer's estate in insolvency. A structured deposit is excluded from the Deposit Insurance Scheme and makes the holder an unsecured creditor of the bank. This is the single most consequential difference between wrappers. The deposit does not rank ahead of fund units and is not DIS-covered.

questions.stem: A bank structures a 3-year note for Mr Goh who invests S$10,000. The reference zero-coupon yield for a 3-year senior unsecured issue is 3.20% per annum. An at-the-money 3-year call on the linked index costs 12.5% of notional. What participation rate does Mr Goh receive, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: Bond cost = S$10,000 / (1.032)^3 = S$10,000 / 1.09911 = S$9,098.30. Option budget = S$10,000 - S$9,098.30 = S$901.70. Option cost in dollars = 12.5% x S$10,000 = S$1,250. Participation rate = S$901.70 / S$1,250 = 72.1%. The 80.2% distractor uses a 3% yield instead of 3.2%. The 90.2% distractor divides the option budget by the bond cost rather than the option premium. The 65.4% distractor applies the participation rate to the bond cost rather than the notional.

questions.stem: A 1-year reverse convertible note of S$50,000 par is linked to a Singapore telco stock at S$4.00 on issue date. The kick-in level is 25% below the issue price. The note pays a 10% coupon. Delivery is 12,500 shares per S$50,000 par if the kick-in is breached. At maturity the share price is S$2.80. What does the investor receive in total?
questions.explanation: Kick-in level = S$4.00 x (1 - 0.25) = S$3.00. At S$2.80 the kick-in IS breached. Investor receives shares: 12,500 x S$2.80 = S$35,000, plus coupon of 10% x S$50,000 = S$5,000. Total = S$40,000. The S$55,000 option assumes the kick-in is not breached (par + coupon). The S$45,000 option uses the wrong share price of S$3.20. The S$35,000 option omits the coupon.

questions.stem: A 2-year bonus certificate on a Singapore property stock is issued at S$3.00. The barrier is continuously monitored at 70% of the issue price. The bonus level is S$3.50. During month 8, the stock dips to S$2.09 then recovers. At maturity the stock is S$3.20. What does the investor receive?
questions.explanation: The barrier is at 70% x S$3.00 = S$2.10. The stock touched S$2.09, breaching the barrier. Once the knock-out is triggered, the bonus protection is permanently lost even if the stock recovers. The investor receives the underlying price at maturity: S$3.20. The S$3.50 option applies the bonus level, which only survives if the barrier is never breached. The S$3.00 issue price and the intraday low are both incorrect.

questions.stem: An airbag certificate is issued at S$40.00 nominal with the airbag level at 35% of spot, S$14.00. At maturity the underlying stock closes at S$10.00. What is the redemption value?
questions.explanation: The final price S$10.00 is below the airbag level S$14.00, so redemption = Nominal x (Final price / Airbag level) = S$40.00 x (10.00 / 14.00) = S$40.00 x 0.7143 = S$28.57. The S$40.00 option applies only at or above the airbag level. The S$14.00 option confuses the airbag level with the payout. The S$10.00 option is the stock price itself, which would apply to a bonus certificate after knock-out, not an airbag certificate.

questions.stem: A client holds a callable structured note. Singapore interest rates have fallen significantly since the note was issued. Which outcome is most likely, and which risk does it illustrate?

options.A: The issuer will call the note and the client must reinvest at lower prevailing rates, illustrating reinvestment risk
options.B: The note price falls because rates have fallen, illustrating market risk
options.C: The client will call the note themselves to lock in a price gain
options.D: The issuer will call the note and pay the client a premium above par as compensation

questions.explanation: The callable feature gives the ISSUER the right to redeem early. When rates fall, the issuer refinances more cheaply by calling the note, and the investor must reinvest proceeds at the lower prevailing yields. This is reinvestment risk. The note's price would RISE when rates fall (not fall), so the market risk distractor is wrong in direction. The client does not hold the call.

questions.stem: Mr Goh invests S$10,000 in a 5-year STI-linked note with 100% capital protection at maturity and a participation rate of 72.1% on the index. At maturity the STI has risen 20% from inception. What is the total payout?
questions.explanation: Payoff = Principal + (Principal x Participation rate x Index return) = S$10,000 + (S$10,000 x 0.721 x 0.20) = S$10,000 + S$1,442 = S$11,442. The S$12,000 option applies the full 20% gain without the participation rate discount. The S$11,200 option applies a 12% gross gain. The S$11,721 distractor uses 72.1% of the full 20% gain correctly but then adds to a wrong principal figure.

questions.stem: Mr Hassan holds S$50,000 of a bank's senior structured notes and S$50,000 of the same bank's subordinated structured notes. The bank is wound up with assets sufficient to repay senior creditors 70 cents in the dollar and nothing thereafter. What does Mr Hassan receive in total?
questions.explanation: Senior debt ranks first. Senior holding: S$50,000 x 70% = S$35,000. Subordinated holding: nothing remains after senior creditors, so S$0. Total = S$35,000. The S$70,000 distractor applies 70% to both holdings. The S$52,500 distractor applies 70% to the senior and 35% to the subordinated. Structured notes are NOT deposit-insured, so the S$50,000 option is wrong.

questions.stem: A discount certificate on a Singapore REIT is issued at S$1.76 (a 12% discount to spot of S$2.00) with a cap-strike of S$2.10. At maturity the REIT is at S$2.40. What does the certificate investor receive and what is the percentage return on the purchase price?
questions.explanation: The REIT price S$2.40 is above the cap-strike S$2.10. The investor receives a cash settlement equal to the cap-strike: S$2.10. Return = (S$2.10 - S$1.76) / S$1.76 = S$0.34 / S$1.76 = 19.3%. The S$2.40 option would apply to a direct REIT investment with no cap. The S$2.00 option confuses the spot price with the payout. The breakeven price is the purchase price S$1.76.

questions.stem: A 5-year note offers 100% capital protection at maturity and a 60% participation rate on the STI. At year 3, the bank that issued the zero-coupon bond component enters judicial management. The product issuer has not provided a separate guarantee. Which risk has crystallised and what is the most likely outcome?

options.A: Market risk: the STI could still fall before maturity
options.B: Correlation risk: the bond and index now move together
options.C: Counterparty credit risk from the bond issuer's failure, which may mean the investor receives less than full principal at maturity even if the index rises
options.D: Liquidity risk: the secondary market for the note will freeze

questions.explanation: Capital protection is provided by the zero-coupon bond. If the bond issuer fails and the product issuer has not given a separate guarantee, the investor is an unsecured creditor of the failed bond issuer and may receive less than full principal at maturity. This is counterparty credit risk from the bond issuer. The index performance is irrelevant to this risk. Liquidity may also suffer but does not explain the principal shortfall.

questions.stem: An adviser recommends a USD-denominated structured note to a Singapore-based client. The note matures at par in USD and the underlying US equity basket rises 30%, giving a strong USD return. However the SGD strengthens 15% against the USD over the term. Which risk most directly reduces the client's SGD-equivalent return?

options.A: Structural risk from embedded leverage in the note
options.B: Correlation risk between the equity basket components
options.C: Early redemption risk if the note is called before maturity
options.D: Foreign exchange risk from converting USD proceeds back to SGD

questions.explanation: The USD return is strong, but the SGD has strengthened 15% against USD, so the conversion back to SGD reduces the investor's real return. This is FX risk operating through the principal conversion and performance measurement channels simultaneously. No barrier or call trigger is mentioned, and correlation risk relates to payoff from multiple underlying assets, not currency conversion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST accurate about structural risk in a structured product?

options.A: Structural risk is completely eliminated by trading the product on an exchange with central clearing
options.B: A kick-in barrier can suddenly expose the investor to full downside losses once breached
options.C: Embedded leverage can amplify losses beyond the underlying asset's percentage move
options.D: Concentration in a small number of reference entities is a form of structural risk

questions.explanation: Exchange listing and central clearing reduce counterparty risk but do not eliminate structural risk. Structural risk is built into the product design, including leverage, barriers, concentration and collateral quality. These product features remain regardless of the listing venue. The other three options all correctly describe structural risk as defined in the study text.

questions.stem: A structured product linked to a basket of five stocks has correlation assumptions built into its pricing model. A market crisis causes all five stocks to become highly positively correlated, moving together more than the model assumed. Which risk category best describes this development?

options.A: Modelling risk only, because correlation is not classified as a separate risk
options.B: Correlation risk: the shift in correlations causes the payoff and the hedge to behave differently than modelled
options.C: Liquidity risk: highly correlated stocks are harder to trade independently
options.D: Legal risk: the product documentation assumed independent stock movements

questions.explanation: Correlation risk is the specific named risk in the study text: it runs from -1 to +1 and when correlations shift, multi-asset structured product payoffs and hedges diverge from the model. Modelling risk is closely related but refers to the model itself breaking down; correlation risk is the named category for this specific scenario. Liquidity and legal risks are separate categories.

questions.stem: An investor holds a 3-year structured note with 100% capital protection and a 70% participation rate. At year 2 she urgently needs cash and unwinds the note. The STI is up 10% from inception. The unwind quote is S$96,200 on a S$100,000 investment. Which best explains why she receives less than principal despite a positive index move?

options.A: The 70% participation rate is applied as a penalty on early redemption
options.B: The capital protection applies only at maturity; the mark-to-market unwind includes a fall in the bond's value from rising yields and a reduction in the option's time value
options.C: The issuer has applied a 3.8% early redemption fee as disclosed in the prospectus
options.D: The STI gain of 10% x 70% = 7% is deducted from the principal on early exit

questions.explanation: Capital protection applies only at the scheduled maturity date. Early redemption triggers a mark-to-market unwind: if yields have risen since issue, the zero-coupon bond's current value is below the invested amount; and the option has lost time value by year 2. Both factors depress the unwind price below par even though the index moved favourably. No early redemption penalty or participation-rate deduction is implied.

questions.stem: An auto-callable structured note pays 8% per annum if all five reference stocks are at or above 100% of initial prices at each annual observation. At the 2-year observation all five stocks clear 100% and the note is automatically redeemed. Similar 3-year notes now offer only 5% per annum. Which risk has materialised?

options.A: Early redemption risk, which is a form of reinvestment risk: the investor must now reinvest at less favourable terms
options.B: Credit risk, because the issuer is repaying early to reduce its obligations
options.C: Market risk, because the stocks rose above their initial prices
options.D: Liquidity risk, because the redemption proceeds may be in an illiquid currency

questions.explanation: Early redemption risk is a specific form of reinvestment risk identified in the study text for callable and auto-callable structures. The investor loses the remaining 3 years of the original 8% and must reinvest at the current 5% offer. No default, currency issue, or market directional risk has materialised; the trigger operated exactly as designed, creating reinvestment risk.

questions.stem: During extreme market stress a designated market-maker on SGX is quoting a structured note bid price 12% below the investor's purchase price. The market-maker is quoting validly but under severe pricing pressure. Which liquidity risk sub-type has occurred?

options.A: Institutional liquidity risk: the market for the instrument has dislocated, making a fair-price exit unavailable
options.B: Investor liquidity risk: the investor personally cannot hold to maturity due to a cash need
options.C: Counterparty credit risk: the market-maker may default
options.D: Modelling risk: the pricing model has over-estimated the bid price

questions.explanation: Institutional liquidity risk is the study text's term for the market for an instrument drying up or becoming dislocated so that fair pricing is unavailable. The market-maker is still quoting (no default) but the bid is severely impaired, fitting the institutional liquidity definition. Investor liquidity risk describes a personal inability to remain invested, not a market pricing failure.

questions.stem: An airline enters a 6-month forward contract to buy jet fuel at US$90 per barrel. At delivery, the spot price is US$105 per barrel. Which statement correctly describes the airline's net cost position?

options.A: The airline pays US$105 spot and loses US$15 per barrel on the forward, net cost US$120
options.B: The airline pays US$90 per barrel under the forward, locking in its budgeted cost regardless of the spot price
options.C: The airline cancels the forward and buys at spot US$105 for a saving relative to the forward
options.D: The airline must pay the higher of spot or forward, so US$105 per barrel

questions.explanation: A forward contract is an obligation on both sides. The airline locked in US$90 per barrel; it pays US$90 under the forward regardless of the US$105 spot price. Either the gain on the settled forward offsets the higher spot purchase, or delivery is taken at US$90 directly. This is a long hedge protecting a future purchase. Forward contracts cannot be unilaterally cancelled.

questions.stem: A fund manager has a Singapore portfolio worth S$1,200,000 with a portfolio beta of 1.5. The STI March futures contract is at 3,200, multiplier S$10 per point. How many contracts must the manager sell to fully hedge the portfolio's market exposure?
questions.explanation: Price coverage per contract = 3,200 x S$10 = S$32,000. Hedge ratio = (Portfolio value / Price coverage) x Beta = (S$1,200,000 / S$32,000) x 1.5 = 37.5 x 1.5 = 56.25, rounded to 56 contracts. The 38-contract distractor comes from ignoring beta (1,200,000 / 32,000 = 37.5). The 48-contract distractor uses beta 1.2 instead of 1.5. The 32-contract distractor divides 1,200,000 by 37,500 instead of 32,000.

questions.stem: Gold spot is S$3,000 per ounce. The 6-month risk-free rate is 4.00% per annum. Combined storage and insurance costs 0.60% per annum of value. What is the 6-month forward price?
questions.explanation: Interest cost over 6 months = S$3,000 x 0.04 x 0.5 = S$60.00. Storage and insurance = S$3,000 x 0.006 x 0.5 = S$9.00. Total carry = S$69.00. Forward price = S$3,000 + S$69 = S$3,069. The S$3,042 distractor adds only storage/insurance and ignores interest. The S$3,057 distractor adds only the interest component. The S$3,079 distractor applies the full annual rates without halving for the 6-month term.

questions.stem: Which of the following is EXCEPT an accurate statement about how futures and forwards differ?

options.A: Futures are exchange-traded and standardised; forwards are OTC and customised
options.B: Futures are marked to market daily; forwards settle P&L only at maturity
options.C: Both futures and forwards require ISDA margin documentation under all circumstances
options.D: A forward price equals spot plus cost of carry and is an arbitrage-free relationship, not a price forecast

questions.explanation: Futures use exchange-mandated margin administered by the clearing house, not ISDA documentation. ISDA agreements with collateral and netting apply to OTC derivatives such as forwards and swaps, and even for OTC contracts ISDA margin is not always required. Options A, B, and D all correctly describe the futures-forward distinction per the study text.

questions.stem: A trader buys 3 stock index futures contracts at 3,000, multiplier S$10 per point. Initial margin S$7,000 per contract; maintenance margin S$5,600 per contract. On Day 1 the index settles at 2,940. What is the margin account balance after Day 1, and is a margin call triggered?
questions.explanation: Initial total margin = 3 x S$7,000 = S$21,000. Maintenance total = 3 x S$5,600 = S$16,800. Day 1 move: (2,940 - 3,000) x S$10 x 3 = -60 x S$10 x 3 = -S$1,800. Balance = S$21,000 - S$1,800 = S$19,200. Since S$19,200 > S$16,800 maintenance, no call is triggered. The S$17,200 distractor uses only 2 contracts. The S$16,800 distractor confuses the maintenance margin with the remaining balance. The S$21,000 distractor shows no change.

questions.stem: A trader buys a long call: 1 contract of 100 shares, strike S$12.00, premium S$1.50 per share. At expiry the stock is S$15.00. What is the net profit on the full contract?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic value at expiry = S$15.00 - S$12.00 = S$3.00 per share. Net profit per share = S$3.00 - S$1.50 premium = S$1.50. Total = S$1.50 x 100 shares = S$150. The S$300 distractor forgets to subtract the premium (S$3.00 x 100). The S$450 distractor uses the full stock price minus the strike without netting the premium. The S$200 distractor applies a wrong intrinsic value.

questions.stem: Michael owns 200 shares of ABC bought at S$8.00. He writes 2 covered call contracts (100 shares each) at a strike of S$8.00 for a premium of S$0.80 per share. At expiry ABC trades at S$11.00. What is Michael's total net profit from the covered call position?
questions.explanation: The calls are exercised. Michael sells shares at the strike S$8.00, which equals his purchase cost, so stock gain = S$0. Premium income = S$0.80 x 200 shares = S$160. Total net gain = S$160. The S$600 distractor treats the position as uncapped (S$3.00 gain x 200). The S$760 distractor adds the premium on top of the uncapped gain. The S$460 distractor uses the stock gain but applies an incorrect premium calculation. The covered call caps the upside at the premium received.

questions.stem: A trader buys a long put on stock ZYX, strike S$10.00, premium S$0.90 per share, 1 contract of 100 shares. ZYX falls to S$7.50 at expiry. What is the net profit?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic value of put = S$10.00 - S$7.50 = S$2.50 per share. Net profit per share = S$2.50 - S$0.90 = S$1.60. Total = S$1.60 x 100 = S$160. The S$250 distractor ignores the premium (S$2.50 x 100). The S$340 distractor adds the premium instead of subtracting it. The S$90 distractor is just the total premium paid, treating the position as a total loss.

questions.stem: An investor simultaneously buys a call and a put on stock PQR, both at strike S$20.00 with the same expiry. The call premium is S$1.20 and the put premium is S$1.00 per share (100 shares per contract). What are the upper and lower breakeven prices at expiry for this long straddle?
questions.explanation: Total premium = S$1.20 + S$1.00 = S$2.20 per share. Upper breakeven = Strike + Total premium = S$20.00 + S$2.20 = S$22.20. Lower breakeven = Strike - Total premium = S$20.00 - S$2.20 = S$17.80. The S$21.20/S$18.80 distractor uses only the call premium. The S$22.00/S$18.00 distractor rounds S$2.20 to S$2.00. The S$21.00/S$19.00 distractor uses only the put premium.

questions.stem: A trader writes (sells) a straddle on stock MNO at strike S$50.00: she sells 1 call and 1 put, each at a premium of S$2.50 per share, on a 100-share contract. At expiry MNO is at S$54.00. What is her net profit or loss?
questions.explanation: Total premium received = (S$2.50 + S$2.50) x 100 = S$500. At S$54.00, the call is exercised against her: loss = (S$54.00 - S$50.00) x 100 = S$400. The put expires worthless: gain = S$0. Net = S$500 premium - S$400 call loss = S$100 profit. Upper breakeven = S$50 + S$5 = S$55; S$54 is inside the upper breakeven, so a profit is made. The S$500 profit distractor ignores the call loss. The S$100 loss distractor gets the direction wrong.

questions.stem: In a credit default swap (CDS), Bank A (the protection buyer) pays 100 basis points per annum on S$5,000,000 notional. The reference entity defaults after exactly 18 months. Bank A did NOT hold any bonds issued by the reference entity. What is the legal position of Bank A's CDS claim?

options.A: Invalid: the protection buyer must own the underlying bond to make a CDS claim
options.B: Valid: a CDS protection buyer need not own the reference asset; the CDS transfers credit risk regardless of whether the buyer holds the bonds
options.C: Valid only if Bank A can demonstrate actual economic loss equal to the bond's fall in market value
options.D: Invalid: CDS contracts terminate automatically when the protection buyer holds no underlying exposure

questions.explanation: A defining and examinable feature of the CDS is that the protection buyer need not own the reference asset. This is precisely what made CDS a speculative tool on credit: one can buy protection against a default without holding the underlying bond. Bank A has paid 18 months of premium and is entitled to the credit-event payment. The 'must own the bond' option states the exact opposite of the CDS rule.

questions.stem: Company X borrows from its bank at LIBOR + 1.00% floating. It then enters an interest rate swap, paying 4.50% fixed and receiving LIBOR. What is Company X's all-in fixed-rate cost of funds after the swap?
questions.explanation: Company X pays its bank LIBOR + 1.00%, pays the swap counterparty 4.50% fixed, and receives LIBOR from the swap. Netting the LIBOR flows: net cost = (LIBOR + 1.00%) + 4.50% - LIBOR = 5.50% fixed. The 4.50% distractor ignores the bank spread. The 6.00% distractor double-counts the 1.00% bank spread. The 3.50% distractor subtracts the bank spread instead of adding it.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes a currency swap from a plain vanilla interest rate swap?

options.A: Both principal and interest are exchanged in full in both directions in a currency swap, with no netting, because the cash flows are in different currencies
options.B: In a currency swap, interest payments on the same dates are netted and only the difference changes hands
options.C: The notional principal is never exchanged in a currency swap
options.D: A currency swap always exchanges a fixed rate for a floating rate, unlike an interest rate swap

questions.explanation: In an interest rate swap the same-currency flows are netted so only the difference changes hands, and principal is never exchanged. In a currency swap, netting is impossible because the flows are in different currencies, so both principal and interest are exchanged in full by both parties at inception and at maturity. The 'principal never exchanged' option describes the interest rate swap, not the currency swap.

questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST characteristic of a contract for differences (CFD)?

options.A: CFDs are leveraged instruments with no fixed expiry date
options.B: A long CFD position receives dividends and pays financing interest
options.C: CFDs can be used to take both long and short positions
options.D: A short CFD position is settled at maturity by physical delivery of shares

questions.explanation: CFDs have no expiry date and always settle in cash; physical delivery is never used. The study text states that CFDs differ from futures and options specifically because they have no expiry dates and are cash-only. Options A, B, and C all accurately describe CFD mechanics per the study text.

questions.stem: An investor buys 100 Apple CFDs at US$200.00 (offer). Margin 5% of notional, commission 0.15% of notional on each side, overnight financing 2.25% per annum on opening notional. She holds for exactly 1 day and closes at US$206.00 (bid). What is the approximate net profit?
questions.explanation: Open notional = 100 x US$200 = US$20,000. Gross profit = 100 x (US$206 - US$200) = US$600. Open commission = US$20,000 x 0.15% = US$30.00. Close commission = US$20,600 x 0.15% = US$30.90. Overnight financing = US$20,000 x 2.25% / 365 = US$1.23. Total costs = US$30.00 + US$30.90 + US$1.23 = US$62.13. Net profit = US$600 - US$62.13 = US$537.87. The US$600 option ignores all costs. The US$569.10 distractor omits one commission leg. The US$480.50 distractor applies the commission rate to the gross profit rather than the notional.

questions.stem: A chooser option allows the holder to elect by a specified choice date whether the option will function as a call or a put. Which scenario would most benefit from a chooser option rather than a long straddle?

options.A: The investor knows the stock will move but wants to pay only one premium rather than two for the same expiry
options.B: The investor expects a very large move in one direction only and wants uncapped upside
options.C: The investor wants to receive dividends and pay financing charges on an open-ended position
options.D: The investor wants to lock in the most favourable price over the entire holding period

questions.explanation: A chooser option pays one premium but lets the holder decide, on the choice date, whether it becomes a call or a put. A straddle buys both a call and a put simultaneously, paying two premiums. When direction is uncertain but a big move is expected, the chooser is more economical than the straddle because only one option premium is paid. The dividend-and-financing description matches a CFD. Locking in the best price over the period describes a lookback option.

questions.stem: Mrs Poh takes up a single-premium structured ILP with a S$80,000 single premium. A 5% front-end charge is immediately deducted from the sub-fund NAV. In month 3 she dies. The sub-fund NAV at that point is S$76,800. The policy provides a death benefit equal to 101% of the single premium or the cash value, whichever is higher. What is the death benefit?
questions.explanation: Death benefit = higher of (101% x S$80,000) or cash value. 101% x S$80,000 = S$80,800. Cash value (NAV) = S$76,800. Since S$80,800 > S$76,800, the death benefit is S$80,800. This shows the insurance layer paying the difference when NAV falls below the guaranteed minimum. The S$82,320 distractor applies 101% to the NAV. The S$78,400 distractor applies 98% to the premium. The S$76,800 distractor is just the NAV.

questions.stem: An adviser tells a prospect: 'Your structured ILP sub-fund is valued daily just like a regular unit trust.' Is this accurate, and what does the study text say?

options.A: Accurate; structured ILP sub-funds are always valued daily as required by MAS Notice 307
options.B: Inaccurate; structured ILP sub-funds need only be valued at least once a month, because derivative contracts are difficult to price reliably on a daily basis
options.C: Inaccurate; structured ILP sub-funds are valued weekly by the independent trustee
options.D: Accurate; the Insurance Act 1966 requires daily NAV publication for all ILP sub-funds

questions.explanation: MAS Notice 307 requires structured ILP sub-funds to be valued at least once a month, not daily. Derivative contracts used in these sub-funds are difficult to price and attach reliable market values to on a daily basis. Regular (non-structured) ILP sub-funds may be valued daily, but the structured variant has a lower monthly minimum, meaning investors may not be able to redeem immediately.

questions.stem: A structured ILP sub-fund has S$8,000,000 NAV and 8,000,000 units. Daily redemption is capped at 10% of units. Total redemption requests on one dealing day are 2,000,000 units. The unit price is S$1.00. Mr Tan submitted a request for 360,000 units. How many units can he redeem today, and what does he receive?
questions.explanation: Daily cap = 10% x 8,000,000 = 800,000 units. Total requests = 2,000,000 units. Pro-rata factor = 800,000 / 2,000,000 = 0.40. Mr Tan's redeemable units = 360,000 x 0.40 = 144,000 units x S$1.00 = S$144,000. His remaining 216,000 units stay invested. The 360,000 option ignores the redemption cap. The 80,000 option applies a 10% deduction directly to Mr Tan's request. The 36,000 option applies a 10% deduction and then a further 10%.

questions.stem: Which combination of documents must a client receive BEFORE purchasing a structured ILP, and which is issued AFTER purchase?

options.A: Before: Policy document only. After: Product Summary and PHS
options.B: Before: Product Summary, Benefit Illustration, PHS. After: Policy document with 14-day free-look right
options.C: Before: Audited Report and PHS. After: Benefit Illustration
options.D: Before: Policy document and Audited Report. After: PHS

questions.explanation: The Product Summary, Benefit Illustration, and Product Highlights Sheet are point-of-sale documents provided before purchase to ensure informed decision-making. The policy document is issued after purchase and triggers the 14-day free-look period during which the client may cancel with a market-value-adjusted refund. The Audited Report and Semi-Annual Report are ongoing post-inception disclosures.

questions.stem: A structured ILP sub-fund has S$60 million NAV. An OTC swap counterparty meeting the minimum long-term credit rating has a mark-to-market exposure of S$7,000,000. A second OTC swap with a below-minimum-rated counterparty has a S$2,800,000 exposure. Which position breaches the Code on CIS concentration limits?

options.B: The lower-rated counterparty swap breaches its 5% cap
options.C: The higher-rated counterparty swap breaches its 10% cap
options.D: Both positions breach their applicable limits

questions.explanation: For counterparties meeting minimum long-term credit rating, the OTC derivative cap is 10% of NAV = 10% x S$60M = S$6,000,000. The S$7,000,000 exposure exceeds this cap. For below-minimum-rated counterparties, the cap is 5% of NAV = S$3,000,000. The S$2,800,000 exposure is within limit. Only the higher-rated counterparty position breaches its limit. The counterintuitive result is that the higher-rated party has the larger absolute cap but the position still breaches it.

questions.stem: An adviser compares a structured ILP (5% front-end charge, 1.5% annual fee, quasi-trust legal structure) with a regular equity unit trust (3% sales charge, 1.0% annual fee, trust legal structure) for a client seeking capital appreciation over 7 years. Which consideration is specific to the structured ILP and not the unit trust?

options.A: The structured ILP sub-fund is legally owned by the insurer; the investor's priority in insolvency derives from the Insurance Act, not from beneficial trust ownership
options.B: The structured ILP sub-fund is regulated by the SFA as a CIS, removing counterparty risk entirely
options.C: The unit trust has a higher front-end charge, making the ILP more cost-effective
options.D: The unit trust has no diversification rules unlike the structured ILP

questions.explanation: The critical ILP-specific distinction is legal ownership. In a unit trust, assets are held by a trustee and investors have beneficial ownership. In a structured ILP, the insurer is the legal owner of the sub-fund assets; investors are not beneficiaries in a trust but have priority claims under the Insurance Act. The ILP also has a HIGHER front-end charge (5% vs 3%), not lower. Both products are subject to diversification rules.

questions.stem: A structured ILP sub-fund reports an expense ratio of 1.60% on a daily average NAV of S$15,000,000. During the year the fund bought S$9,000,000 of securities and sold S$7,500,000. What are the annual operating expenses and the turnover ratio?
questions.explanation: Operating expenses = 1.60% x S$15,000,000 = S$240,000. Turnover ratio = lesser of purchases or sales divided by daily average NAV = S$7,500,000 / S$15,000,000 = 50%. The lesser of S$9M (purchases) and S$7.5M (sales) is S$7.5M. Using the larger purchases figure (S$9M / S$15M = 60%) is the common wrong answer. The S$200,000 options apply an incorrect expense ratio.

questions.stem: Under the Code on CIS, which activity is EXCEPT permitted for a retail structured ILP sub-fund?

options.A: Investing in liquid equities and bonds subject to the single-entity concentration limits
options.B: Entering OTC financial derivative transactions with a regulated counterparty subject to prudential supervision
options.C: Lending money to the fund manager to fund redemptions during a liquidity crunch
options.D: Investing in cash and money market instruments for liquidity management

questions.explanation: The Code on CIS explicitly prohibits retail CIS sub-funds from lending money or granting guarantees. Lending to the fund manager is a prohibited activity regardless of the purpose. Investing in equities and bonds within concentration limits, OTC derivatives with regulated counterparties, and cash instruments are all permitted.

questions.stem: Mr Raj purchased a structured ILP with a S$120,000 single premium. On day 8 he cancels within the 14-day free-look period. The unit price fell from S$1.00 at purchase to S$0.96 at cancellation. How much does he receive?

options.A: S$120,000 plus accrued interest for 8 days
options.B: S$120,000, because the free-look period guarantees a full refund
options.C: S$114,000, because the front-end charge is retained on cancellation
options.D: S$115,200, because the refund is adjusted for the downward market movement in unit price

questions.explanation: The free-look refund is adjusted downward for market price movements in the NAV per unit. If 120,000 units were allocated at S$1.00 and the unit price falls to S$0.96, the refund is 120,000 x S$0.96 = S$115,200. The full S$120,000 refund would apply only if prices had not fallen. The market value adjustment runs one way: downward falls reduce the refund, but upward moves do not increase it above the premium paid.

questions.stem: A client with S$500,000 wants to appoint her own choice of fund managers and access equities, bonds, and CIS within a single insurance wrapper. Her investment horizon is 4 years. Which statement best describes the adviser's suitability assessment?

options.A: A portfolio bond is suitable because it offers the broadest investment choice and flexibility
options.B: A portfolio bond is unsuitable primarily because a 4-year horizon is too short for the higher charges to be recovered; the cost-benefit is unlikely to be attractive
options.C: A portfolio bond is suitable because the tax advantages will outweigh the charges over 4 years
options.D: A portfolio bond is suitable if the client selects lower-fee fund managers within the wrapper

questions.explanation: The study text explicitly states portfolio bonds are unsuitable for investors with a 3 to 5-year horizon because the higher front-end and ongoing charges need more time to be recovered. A 4-year horizon falls squarely in that unsuitable range. Wide investment choice is a feature, not a suitability override. Tax advantages can be outweighed by costs and may change.

questions.stem: A portfolio bond policy owner carries a product charge of 0.70%, fund charge of 1.10%, and embedded mortality charge of 0.15% annually. The portfolio is worth S$300,000. What is the approximate total annual cost in dollars, and what specifically does the mortality charge pay for?

options.A: S$5,850; paying for the portfolio rebalancing service
options.B: S$4,500; paying for the consolidated fund manager reporting system
options.C: S$5,850; paying for the small death benefit embedded in the insurance wrapper
options.D: S$4,500; paying for the surrender charge protection

questions.explanation: Total annual charge = 0.70% + 1.10% + 0.15% = 1.95%. Annual cost = S$300,000 x 1.95% = S$5,850. The mortality charge is an annual charge specifically for death benefits, the insurance element that makes the product a life policy. It does not pay for rebalancing, reporting integration, or surrender-charge protection.

questions.stem: A portfolio bond investor receives a regular monthly payment of S$3,000. He describes this to a friend as 'my bond income'. Which aspect of this description is LEAST accurate?

options.A: The payment is not income in the sense of interest; it is funded by redeeming (selling) units, which reduces the invested capital base
options.B: The payments are not guaranteed and depend on the unit price at the time of redemption
options.C: The portfolio bond does not pay coupons the way a conventional bond does; its value tracks underlying investments, not interest rates
options.D: The payment is tax-free in Singapore in all circumstances because portfolio bonds enjoy blanket insurance wrapper tax treatment

questions.explanation: The LEAST accurate claim is the blanket tax-free assertion. Tax treatment depends on the investor's jurisdiction and personal tax position; the study text notes that tax laws can change and the portfolio bond's cost of ownership may outweigh tax benefits. Options A, B, and C correctly describe the mechanics: the payment is unit redemption, it is not guaranteed, and a portfolio bond is not a conventional bond.

questions.stem: A portfolio bond policy owner instructs a gradual switch of S$48,000 from an equity fund to a bond fund over 6 monthly tranches of S$8,000 each. This describes which portfolio bond feature, and how does it differ from portfolio rebalancing?

options.A: Drip-feeding: a fund switch in small doses to avoid market disruption; rebalancing restores a drifted allocation automatically on a set schedule
options.B: Portfolio rebalancing: restoring the 50/50 allocation that drifted to 63/37; drip-feeding is done in a single large trade
options.C: A surrender charge trigger: switching more than once a year incurs a penalty in most portfolio bonds
options.D: Mortality charge adjustment: switching funds changes the death benefit calculation

questions.explanation: Drip-feeding implements a fund switch in small doses over time to avoid market disruption from a large single trade. Portfolio rebalancing is different: it restores an original risk allocation that has drifted through market movements, and can run automatically monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or annually. The scenario describes an intentional gradual move, not a drift correction.

questions.stem: In the Superior Income Plan (SIP), a policy owner invests S$10,000. In policy year 2, all six reference stocks trade consistently between 92% and 108% of their initial prices on every trading day (n = N = 250). What is the annual payout, and which payout formula applies?

options.A: S$400; the guaranteed 4% floor applies because the non-guaranteed formula gives exactly 4%
options.B: S$1,000; the non-guaranteed formula gives 10% because stocks averaged 100% of initial price
options.C: S$2,000; the non-guaranteed formula gives 20% (20% x 250/250) which exceeds the 4% floor
options.D: S$800; the guaranteed 4% floor doubles because all stocks held above 92%

questions.explanation: Annual payout = higher of (4% guaranteed) or (20% x n/N). With n = N = 250, the non-guaranteed result is 20% x 250/250 = 20%. Since 20% > 4%, the non-guaranteed 20% applies. Payout = S$10,000 x 20% = S$2,000. This is Scenario 3 in the case study and the BEST outcome for the policy owner: stocks staying inside the 92-108% band is what the policy owner wants, because breaching 108% triggers early redemption and cuts the policy short.

questions.stem: In the SIP, the early redemption trigger fires 6 months into the policy when all six stocks reach 108% of their initial prices. Assuming 250 trading days in a full year and 125 elapsed, what is the total amount received by the policy owner on a S$10,000 single premium?

options.A: S$11,000; the non-guaranteed pro-rata payout is 20% x 125/250 = 10%, giving S$1,000 plus S$10,000 principal
options.B: S$10,480; the pro-rata non-guaranteed rate is 4.8% (20% x 60/250), applied at 3 months not 6
options.C: S$10,800; the 108% trigger means the policy returns premium plus 8%
options.D: S$10,400; the guaranteed 4% annual rate is applied in full regardless of days elapsed

questions.explanation: Pro-rata non-guaranteed payout = 20% x (125/250) = 10%. Pro-rata guaranteed = 4% x (125/250) = 2%. Since 10% > 2%, the non-guaranteed applies. Payout = S$10,000 x 10% = S$1,000. Total = S$10,000 principal + S$1,000 = S$11,000. The 108% figure is a REDEMPTION TRIGGER, not a return amount. The S$10,800 distractor treats 108% as an 8% return, which the study text explicitly warns against.

questions.stem: In the Lifestyle Plan case study, the Choice Fund has a Secure Price of S$1.00455 per unit. At maturity, the NAV per unit is S$0.9293. A policy owner holds 10,000 units. What is the maturity payout and why?

options.A: S$10,045.50; the Secure Price is a guaranteed floor the insurer must honour
options.B: S$10,000.00; the policy always returns premiums paid at maturity
options.C: S$10,045.50; in any capital-guaranteed ILP fund the payout is always the higher of NAV and guaranteed amount
options.D: S$9,293.00; the Secure Price is an aspiration, not a guarantee; payout is based on the unit NAV

questions.explanation: The Secure Price is NOT a guaranteed floor; it is an investment target the manager strives to achieve. If the NAV per unit at maturity is S$0.9293, which is below the Secure Price, the payout is based on the actual unit price: 10,000 x S$0.9293 = S$9,293. The capital-guaranteed ILP rule (payout = higher of NAV and guaranteed amount) applies only to explicitly capital-guaranteed products, not to the Choice Fund whose Secure Price is discretionary.

questions.stem: An adviser presents two products to a client worried about issuer insolvency risk: (A) a structured ILP, where the insurer is the legal owner of the sub-fund assets; and (B) a structured fund (CIS unit trust), where assets are held by an independent trustee. Which statement correctly contrasts their protection against the issuing entity's insolvency?

options.A: Both provide identical protection because both comply with the CIS Code investment restrictions
options.B: The structured ILP gives stronger protection because the Insurance Act gives policy owners priority over all other creditors in liquidation
options.C: The structured fund gives stronger protection because the trustee holds assets independently of the fund manager's balance sheet; the ILP sub-fund investor relies on the Insurance Act priority rather than true beneficial trust ownership
options.D: Neither provides any protection because both are unsecured creditors of their respective issuers

questions.explanation: In a structured fund (CIS trust), assets are held by an independent trustee, so they are off the fund manager's balance sheet and investors are beneficial owners. In a structured ILP, the insurer is the legal owner of sub-fund assets; investors are not beneficial owners in a trust sense but have a statutory priority claim under the Insurance Act if the insurer is wound up. The trust structure provides more direct protection from fund manager insolvency than the quasi-trust ILP structure.

questions.stem: Priya invests S$50,000 in a 3-year capital-return note. The zero-coupon yield for the bond component is 2.80% per annum. How much of her S$50,000 must be placed in the zero-coupon bond today so that it grows back to S$50,000 at maturity?
questions.explanation: Bond cost = 50,000 / (1.028)^3. (1.028)^2 = 1.056784; x 1.028 = 1.086374. Bond cost = 50,000 / 1.086374 = S$46,026. The S$43,071 figure comes from (1.038)^4, the wrong rate and term. The S$48,500 figure omits compounding. The S$44,933 figure uses an incorrect rate.

questions.stem: Using the same S$50,000 note (3-year, 2.80% ZC yield, so S$46,026 in the zero-coupon bond), the remaining S$3,974 is available for the option sleeve. The dealer quotes the at-the-money 3-year call at 13% of the notional investment. What is the participation rate?
questions.explanation: Option budget = S$3,974. Option cost = 50,000 x 13% = S$6,500. Participation rate = 3,974 / 6,500 = 61.1%. The 79.5% figure uses an incorrect option cost of S$5,000. The 30.6% figure halves the budget by mistake. 100% would require the option budget to equal the full option cost, which it does not.

questions.stem: Gold spot is S$3,100 per ounce. The 6-month risk-free rate is 3.60% per annum and combined storage and insurance costs 0.40% per annum of value. What is the correct 6-month forward price per ounce?
questions.explanation: Interest over 6 months = 3,100 x 0.036 x 0.5 = S$55.80. Storage and insurance = 3,100 x 0.004 x 0.5 = S$6.20. Forward price = 3,100 + 55.80 + 6.20 = S$3,162.00. The S$3,155.80 figure omits storage and insurance. The S$3,168.20 figure applies a blended rate of 4.40% incorrectly. S$3,100 ignores cost of carry entirely.

questions.stem: An equity index sits at 3,800 points. The 3-month funding rate is 3.20% per annum and the dividend yield is 4.80% per annum. What is the 3-month forward price, and is the index in contango or backwardation?

options.A: Forward = 3,814.6; contango because financing exceeds dividends
options.B: Forward = 3,800.0; always at spot for equity indices
options.C: Forward = 3,830.4; contango because dividends exceed financing
options.D: Forward = 3,784.8; backwardation because dividends exceed financing

questions.explanation: Financing cost = 3,800 x 0.032 x 0.25 = 30.4 points. Dividend receipts = 3,800 x 0.048 x 0.25 = 45.6 points. Net carry = 30.4 - 45.6 = -15.2 points. Forward = 3,800 - 15.2 = 3,784.8. Because dividends exceed financing, the forward is below spot, which is backwardation. The 3,814.6 figure adds dividends rather than subtracting them. The 3,830.4 ignores dividends entirely.

questions.stem: Farhan buys 3 stock index futures at 4,600 points, multiplier S$20 per point. Initial margin is S$12,000 per contract and maintenance margin is S$9,600 per contract. Day 1 settles at 4,560; Day 2 settles at 4,475. How much variation margin must Farhan pay at the end of Day 2?
questions.explanation: Total initial margin = 3 x 12,000 = S$36,000. Total maintenance = 3 x 9,600 = S$28,800. Day 1 loss = (4,600-4,560) x 20 x 3 = 40 x 60 = S$2,400. Balance = 36,000 - 2,400 = S$33,600, above maintenance, no call. Day 2 loss = (4,560-4,475) x 20 x 3 = 85 x 60 = S$5,100. Balance = 33,600 - 5,100 = S$28,500, below S$28,800, margin call triggered. Variation margin restores to initial: 36,000 - 28,500 = S$9,900. The S$7,500 figure is the Day 2 loss alone, not the top-up amount. The S$2,400 is only the Day 1 loss.

questions.stem: Under MAS requirements in force since September 2009, which statement about the marketing of structured products in Singapore is CORRECT?

options.A: Products may be described as 'capital protected' as long as a footnote discloses the risks
options.B: The terms 'capital protected' and 'capital guaranteed' may be used interchangeably for any product with a bond component
options.C: A product may not be marketed as 'capital protected' or 'capital guaranteed' unless the capital is genuinely guaranteed
options.D: The restriction applies only to structured deposits, not structured notes

questions.explanation: Since September 2009, issuers in Singapore may not label a product 'capital protected' or 'capital guaranteed' unless it genuinely is. The rule followed the Lehman Minibond collapse, applies across structured products rather than a single wrapper, and a risk footnote does not cure a misleading label.

questions.stem: Wei Ling holds a portfolio worth S$2,400,000 with a portfolio beta of 1.35. She wants a short hedge using STI futures trading at 5,800 points with a multiplier of S$10 per point. How many contracts should she sell, rounded to the nearest whole number?
questions.explanation: Price coverage per contract = 5,800 x S$10 = S$58,000. Hedge ratio = (2,400,000 / 58,000) x 1.35 = 41.379 x 1.35 = 55.86, rounded to 56 contracts. The 41 figure omits the beta adjustment entirely. The 62 figure applies beta 1.5 in error. The 44 figure uses an incorrect price coverage per contract.

questions.stem: Ng buys a call option on Singtel shares: strike S$46, premium S$3.20 per share, contract size 500 shares. At expiry the share price is S$54. What is Ng's total net profit on the contract?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic value per share at expiry = 54 - 46 = S$8.00. Net profit per share = 8.00 - 3.20 = S$4.80. Total = 500 x 4.80 = S$2,400. The S$4,000 figure ignores the premium (8 x 500). The S$1,600 figure uses an incorrect intrinsic value. The S$5,600 adds the premium to the payoff instead of deducting it.

questions.stem: Which statement about the risk positions of option buyers and option writers is CORRECT?

options.A: The buyer's maximum loss is unlimited, while the writer's loss is capped at the premium
options.B: The buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid, while the writer of an uncovered call faces potentially unlimited loss
options.C: Both the buyer and the writer face losses capped at the premium
options.D: The writer of a put faces unlimited loss because share prices can rise without limit

questions.explanation: An option buyer can lose no more than the premium paid. An uncovered call writer must deliver stock at the strike however high the market rises, so the potential loss is unlimited. A put writer's loss is large but limited, because a share price cannot fall below zero.

questions.stem: Lim buys a put option: strike S$38, premium S$2.50, contract size 200 shares. At expiry the share price is S$29. What is Lim's total net profit on the put position?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic value = 38 - 29 = S$9.00. Net profit per share = 9.00 - 2.50 = S$6.50. Total = 200 x 6.50 = S$1,300. The S$1,800 figure uses the full intrinsic value without deducting the premium (9 x 200 = 1,800). The S$1,000 figure uses an incorrect intrinsic value of S$7.50. The S$1,900 figure adds the premium to the gross payoff instead of deducting it.

questions.stem: Rajan owns 1,000 shares of Keppel Corp purchased at S$28.00 per share. He writes a covered call at a strike of S$30.00 and receives a premium of S$1.80 per share. At expiry the share price is S$35.00. What is Rajan's net profit per share on the combined position?
questions.explanation: The call is exercised at S$30.00. Capital gain vs cost = 30.00 - 28.00 = S$2.00 per share. Add premium received = S$1.80. Net profit = S$3.80. The S$7.00 figure is the unhedged stock gain at S$35 minus cost, ignoring the call cap at S$30. The S$1.80 is the premium alone, omitting the capital gain. There is no loss on this covered call at S$35.

questions.stem: A wheat farmer sells wheat futures to protect the value of an upcoming harvest. A fund manager with no wheat exposure buys wheat futures purely because he expects prices to rise. Which classification of the two parties is CORRECT?

options.C: The farmer is a speculator and the fund manager is a hedger
options.D: The farmer is a short hedger and the fund manager is a speculator

questions.explanation: A hedger uses derivatives to reduce an existing or anticipated exposure; selling futures against a crop you will hold is a short hedge. Taking a position with no underlying exposure, purely to profit from an expected price move, is speculation.

questions.stem: Siti owns 800 shares of SIA purchased at S$8.50. She buys a protective put with a strike of S$7.50 and pays S$0.60 per share. The shares fall to S$5.20 at expiry. What is Siti's net loss per share on the combined position?
questions.explanation: The put is exercised at S$7.50. Loss on stock from purchase price down to the put strike = 8.50 - 7.50 = S$1.00. The put premium is an additional cost. Maximum loss = 1.00 + 0.60 = S$1.60 per share, fixed regardless of how far the stock falls below S$7.50. The S$0.60 is the premium alone. The S$3.30 is the unhedged stock loss (8.50 - 5.20). The S$2.00 omits the premium.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly states the SGX listing thresholds for exchange-traded products?

options.A: An ETF must have at least S$20 million in assets, with 25% held by at least 500 public holders, while an ETN needs an issue size of at least S$750,000
options.B: An ETF must have at least S$750,000 in assets, while an ETN needs an issue size of at least S$20 million
options.C: Both ETFs and ETNs must have at least S$20 million in assets and 1,000 public holders
options.D: An ETF has no minimum asset requirement provided it has at least 500 public holders

questions.explanation: SGX requires an ETF to hold at least S$20 million in assets with 25% spread across at least 500 public holders, while an ETN needs a minimum issue size of S$750,000. The minimums exist to support liquidity and orderly trading.

questions.stem: Aisha enters a plain vanilla interest rate swap on S$8,000,000 notional: she pays fixed 4.20% per annum and receives SIBOR. The current semi-annual SIBOR rate is 3.50% per annum. What is the net cash flow for Aisha this period?
questions.explanation: Fixed payment = 8,000,000 x 4.20% x 0.5 = S$168,000. Floating receipt = 8,000,000 x 3.50% x 0.5 = S$140,000. Net payment = 168,000 - 140,000 = S$28,000. Because Aisha's fixed rate exceeds the floating rate, she is the net payer. Interest rate swaps in the same currency net the cash flows. The S$168,000 ignores the floating receipt. The S$140,000 is the receipt alone. She is a net payer, not a net receiver.

questions.stem: Cost-Cutter Airlines enters a commodity swap paying fixed US$95 per barrel and receiving the Platts jet fuel index. This quarter the volume is 400,000 barrels and the Platts index settles at US$108. Who pays whom, and how much?

options.A: The airline pays the bank US$5,200,000
options.B: The bank pays the airline US$5,200,000
options.C: The airline pays the bank US$3,800,000
options.D: The bank pays the airline US$700,000

questions.explanation: When the Platts floating price (US$108) exceeds the fixed rate (US$95), the bank pays the airline. Net settlement = (108 - 95) x 400,000 = 13 x 400,000 = US$5,200,000 received by the airline. This offsets the extra cost of buying physical fuel at US$108 against the budgeted US$95. The US$3,800,000 multiplies the fixed rate by volume incorrectly. The US$700,000 applies the wrong differential.

questions.stem: Farhan buys 200 CFDs on ABC stock at an offer price of S$18.50. His broker requires 5% margin and charges a financing rate of SIBOR (2.00%) + 2.50% per annum. After 3 days he closes at a bid of S$19.80. Ignoring commissions, what is his approximate net profit after 3 days of financing costs?
questions.explanation: Gross profit = 200 x (19.80 - 18.50) = 200 x 1.30 = S$260.00. Notional = 200 x 18.50 = S$3,700. Daily financing = 3,700 x 0.045 / 365 = S$0.4562. For 3 days = S$1.37. Net profit = 260.00 - 1.37 = S$258.63. The S$261.37 adds the financing cost instead of deducting it. The S$260.00 ignores financing entirely. The S$259.99 uses a different financing rate.

questions.stem: A S$60,000 par reverse convertible note pays an 8.50% annual coupon. It is linked to a stock trading at S$64 at issue. The kick-in level is 25% below the issue price. At maturity the stock is at S$42. What does the investor receive in total?
questions.explanation: Kick-in level = 64 x 0.75 = S$48. Since S$42 is below S$48, the kick-in is breached. Delivery ratio = 60,000 / 64 = 937.5 shares. Share delivery value = 937.5 x 42 = S$39,375. Annual coupon = 60,000 x 8.50% = S$5,100. Total = 39,375 + 5,100 = S$44,475. The S$65,100 figure incorrectly pays par plus coupon as if the kick-in were not breached. The S$39,375 omits the coupon. The S$49,575 uses the wrong share price.

questions.stem: A discount certificate on a Singapore-listed tech stock is purchased at S$5.20. The cap-strike is S$6.40. At maturity the stock trades at S$7.80. What does the investor receive and what is the approximate percentage return?
questions.explanation: When the stock price exceeds the cap-strike at maturity, the investor receives the cap-strike in cash. Payout = S$6.40. Return = (6.40 - 5.20) / 5.20 = 1.20 / 5.20 = 23.08%, approximately 23.1%. The S$7.80 payout ignores the cap. The 15.4% return divides by S$7.80 instead of the purchase price.

questions.stem: An airbag certificate is issued at S$60 nominal on a stock at S$60. The airbag level is 30% of the issue price (S$18). At maturity the stock price is S$12. What is the redemption value per certificate?
questions.explanation: Since S$12 is below the airbag level of S$18, the formula applies: redemption = nominal x (final price / airbag level) = 60 x (12 / 18) = 60 x 0.6667 = S$40.00. This is above the S$12 the share itself is worth, which is the airbag's protective effect. The S$12 ignores the airbag cushion. The S$18 confuses the airbag level with the redemption amount. The S$60 nominal is only paid when the stock is at or above the airbag level.

questions.stem: The Superior Income Plan (SIP) has N = 250 trading days in a year. In year 3, all six reference stocks were at or above 92% of their initial prices on n = 195 trading days. A policy owner has a S$15,000 single premium. What annual payout does he receive for year 3?
questions.explanation: Non-guaranteed payout rate = 20% x (195 / 250) = 20% x 0.78 = 15.6%. Payout = 15,000 x 15.6% = S$2,340. The guaranteed floor = 15,000 x 4% = S$600. Since S$2,340 exceeds S$600, the higher figure applies. The S$3,000 applies 20% without the n/N adjustment. The S$780 misapplies 4% x (n/N) = 4% x 0.78 = 3.12%, which incorrectly applies the floor rate to the ratio.

questions.stem: A S$20,000 SIP policy is triggered for early redemption by ABC Insurance after 60 trading days (approximately 3 months), when all six stocks reach or exceed 108% of their initial prices. The year has N = 250 trading days. What total amount does the policy owner receive?
questions.explanation: Non-guaranteed pro-rata payout rate = 20% x (60 / 250) = 4.8%. Since 4.8% exceeds the guaranteed floor of 4%, the payout is 20,000 x 4.8% = S$960. Total received = single premium S$20,000 + payout S$960 = S$20,960. The S$21,600 figure applies 8%, confusing the 108% trigger level with the return percentage. The S$24,000 applies the full annual 20% rate as if held for a full year.

questions.stem: In the SIP, all six reference stocks remain consistently between 92% and 108% of their initial prices for all five years (the moderate market scenario). A policy owner has a S$10,000 single premium. What is the total amount received over the full policy term?
questions.explanation: When n = N every trading day, the non-guaranteed payout rate = 20% x N/N = 20%. Annual payout = 10,000 x 20% = S$2,000. Over 5 years, total payouts = 5 x S$2,000 = S$10,000. At maturity the S$10,000 single premium is also repaid. Total = S$10,000 + S$10,000 = S$20,000. The S$12,000 result applies the guaranteed 4% floor scenario (S$400 x 5 + S$10,000). The S$14,000 and S$15,000 use incorrect payout rates.

questions.stem: On a S$10,000 SIP single premium, a 5% initial fee is deducted from the NAV immediately. What percentage return must the remaining invested capital earn in the first year just to restore the NAV to S$10,000?
questions.explanation: After the 5% fee, the fund NAV = 10,000 x 0.95 = S$9,500. Required gain = (10,000 - 9,500) / 9,500 = 500 / 9,500 = 5.263%, rounded to 5.26%. The 5.00% measures the fee as a percentage of the original premium, not of the money actually in the market. The 4.76% is an inverted ratio. The study text states the shorthand of 'earn 8%' is the charge measured against the original premium, but the actual return on invested capital required is higher.

questions.stem: The Choice Fund (Case Study 2) has a NAV per unit of S$0.9293 and a Secure Price of S$1.00455. A client pays a S$8,000 single premium and a 5% front-end charge is deducted. How many units does the client hold?
questions.explanation: Net amount invested after 5% charge = 8,000 x 0.95 = S$7,600. Units = 7,600 / 0.9293 = 8,178.20. The 8,000 unit figure divides the gross premium by the NAV, ignoring the 5% front-end charge. The 7,556.44 figure divides S$7,600 by the Secure Price instead of the NAV per unit. The 8,392.10 figure uses an incorrect NAV.

questions.stem: Which of the following lists only charges that are typically levied on a portfolio bond (insurance wrapper)?

options.A: Product charge, Deposit Insurance levy, brokerage stamp fee, smoothing charge
options.B: Bonus smoothing charge, par fund levy, surrender charge, payment charge
options.C: Mortality charge, terminal bonus deduction, product charge, guaranteed coupon fee
options.D: Product charge, surrender charge, valuation charge, mortality charge

questions.explanation: The portfolio bond fee stack typically includes product charges, fund charges and transaction costs, early withdrawal and surrender charges, valuation and payment charges, dealing account debit interest, and a mortality charge. Deposit Insurance levies and bonus smoothing belong to other product types; a portfolio bond has no smoothing or par-fund mechanics and pays no guaranteed coupon.

questions.stem: A structured ILP sub-fund has 10,000,000 units outstanding at S$1.20 each (NAV = S$12,000,000). The fund applies a daily redemption cap of 10% of units outstanding. On one dealing day, requests totalling 3,000,000 units arrive. A policy owner submitted a request for 150,000 units. How many units does he actually redeem that day?
questions.explanation: Daily redemption cap = 10% x 10,000,000 = 1,000,000 units. Pro-rata factor = 1,000,000 / 3,000,000 = 1/3 = 33.33%. This policy owner redeems 150,000 x 1/3 = 50,000 units, worth S$60,000 at S$1.20. The remaining 100,000 units stay invested. The 150,000 figure ignores the cap entirely. The 100,000 applies a 2/3 ratio in error. The 60,000 assumes an incorrect 40% pro-rata.

questions.stem: A structured ILP sub-fund reports operating expenses of S$168,000 for the year and a daily average NAV of S$9,600,000. The fund bought S$7,200,000 and sold S$5,400,000 of securities during the year. What are the expense ratio and the turnover ratio?
questions.explanation: Expense ratio = 168,000 / 9,600,000 = 1.75%. The turnover ratio uses the LESSER of purchases or sales as numerator: min(7,200,000; 5,400,000) = 5,400,000. Turnover ratio = 5,400,000 / 9,600,000 = 56.25%. Using the larger purchases figure gives 75%, a common error. The 1.50% expense ratio uses an incorrect denominator.

questions.stem: On a dual-priced ILP sub-fund, offer price is S$1.0800 and bid price is S$1.0300. Wei Ling uses a chargeable switch (bid-to-offer) to move 40,000 units from Fund A (same prices) into Fund B (same prices). How many units does she receive in Fund B?
questions.explanation: Sell Fund A at bid: 40,000 x S$1.0300 = S$41,200. Buy Fund B at offer: 41,200 / S$1.0800 = 38,148.15 units. On a free switch (bid-to-bid) she would receive 40,000 units, keeping the same count. The chargeable switch costs 40,000 - 38,148.15 = 1,851.85 fewer units. The 39,259.26 figure uses an incorrect spread. The 40,000 units result is from the free switch, not the chargeable one.

questions.stem: The SIP policy document states that XYZ Bank's guarantee terminates if XYZ goes into liquidation. Without that explicit termination clause, what would the legal position be?

options.A: XYZ Bank would still be fully liable even in liquidation because guarantees are irrevocable
options.B: ABC Insurance, as the primary insurer and party to the insurance contract, would be obligated to honour the guaranteed 4% payout and capital repayment even if XYZ Bank failed
options.C: MAS would step in to fund the guarantee from the Policy Owners Protection Scheme
options.D: The policy owner would have no claim on anyone if both XYZ and ABC became insolvent

questions.explanation: Without the explicit termination clause, ABC Insurance, as the primary party to the insurance contract, would be contractually obligated to honour the guaranteed floor and capital repayment regardless of XYZ Bank's fate. The clause is precisely what transfers the counterparty risk from ABC to the investor's exposure to XYZ. MAS does not guarantee structured ILP payouts through the Policy Owners Protection Scheme.

questions.stem: A long straddle is built on a stock at S$72: buy one call (premium S$4.20) and one put (premium S$3.80), both with the S$72 strike. At what two prices does the position break even at expiry?
questions.explanation: Total premium paid = 4.20 + 3.80 = S$8.00. Upper breakeven = 72 + 8 = S$80.00. Lower breakeven = 72 - 8 = S$64.00. The S$67.80 / S$76.20 pair uses only the call premium. The S$68.00 / S$76.00 pair uses only the put premium. The S$63.60 / S$80.40 pair uses S$8.40 as the total, an arithmetic error.

questions.stem: In a callable structured security, which party holds the embedded call option, and what is the main risk this creates for the investor?

options.A: The investor holds the call and can redeem early whenever rates rise
options.B: The issuer holds the call, so the investor faces reinvestment risk if rates fall and the security is called
options.C: The clearing house holds the call in order to manage margin risk
options.D: The issuer holds the call, which protects the investor against falling interest rates

questions.explanation: A callable security is valued as a straight bond minus a call option held by the issuer. When interest rates fall, the issuer redeems early and the investor must reinvest the proceeds at the new, lower rates. The investor is effectively short the call and carries the reinvestment risk.

questions.stem: All of the following correctly distinguish currency swaps from interest rate swaps EXCEPT one. Which statement is LEAST accurate?

options.A: Currency swaps exchange both principal and interest; interest rate swaps exchange only the net interest difference
options.B: Currency swaps involve two different currencies; interest rate swaps operate in the same currency
options.C: Interest rate swaps net the cash flows because both legs are in the same currency; currency swaps pay full interest on both legs
options.D: Currency swaps are always exchange-traded while interest rate swaps are always over-the-counter

questions.explanation: Both currency swaps and interest rate swaps are predominantly OTC instruments. Neither is restricted to exchange-traded or OTC execution exclusively. All other statements correctly describe the distinction: currency swaps exchange principal at inception and maturity and pay full interest on both legs without netting, whereas interest rate swaps in the same currency net the cash flows and never exchange principal.

questions.stem: Ng, a portfolio manager, buys credit protection on a corporate bond issuer without owning any of the issuer's bonds. Which derivative makes this possible and why?

options.A: A credit default swap; because the CDS protection buyer does not need to own the reference asset, enabling a pure credit view
options.B: An equity swap; because equity swaps can reference any asset class including credit
options.C: A swaption; because it gives the right to enter any underlying swap
options.D: An interest rate futures contract; because it trades credit spreads on exchange

questions.explanation: A CDS transfers credit risk from buyer to seller for a periodic premium. The protection buyer need NOT own the underlying bond or loan, which is the feature that allows pure credit speculation. Equity swaps reference equity returns, not credit risk. A swaption gives the right to enter an interest rate or other swap. Credit default swaps are OTC instruments, not exchange-traded interest rate futures.

questions.stem: Priya holds a SHORT CFD position in a Singapore REIT. Which statement about her cash flow treatment is LEAST accurate?

options.A: She receives interest adjustments because she is effectively borrowing and short-selling a financed position
options.B: There is no fixed expiry date on the CFD
options.C: She pays dividends to the CFD provider when the REIT distributes income
options.D: She pays financing interest on the notional value of the position each day it remains open

questions.explanation: A SHORT CFD position receives interest (not pays it) and pays dividends. Paying financing interest on the notional value describes a LONG CFD position. The short CFD holder benefits from the interest credit because she is effectively lending the notional proceeds of the short sale. All other statements correctly describe a short CFD: receiving interest, no expiry, and paying dividends.

questions.stem: A bonus certificate on a Singapore airline stock is issued at S$6.00 with a continuously monitored barrier at 70% of spot (S$4.20) and a bonus level of S$7.50. During the certificate's life the stock briefly touches S$4.15 before recovering to S$6.40 at maturity. What does the investor receive at maturity?
questions.explanation: The barrier at S$4.20 was breached when the stock touched S$4.15. On a continuously monitored barrier, once knock-out occurs the bonus protection is removed for the remainder of the certificate's life regardless of any price recovery. The investor receives the underlying price at maturity, S$6.40, not the bonus level of S$7.50. The barrier-touch price of S$4.15 is not locked in as the payout.

questions.stem: Lim wants an option that lets him lock in a profit while the option is in the money during its life, and still participate in any further upside. Which exotic option type fits his objective?
questions.explanation: A shout option lets the holder lock in (shout) a certain profit level when the option is in the money before expiry, then continue to participate in any further favourable move until expiry. The Asian option uses average prices but does not allow mid-life lock-in. The lookback selects the most favourable price at expiry only, not during the life. The compound option gives the right to purchase another option.

questions.stem: A fund manager uses an equity swap to gain exposure to a foreign equity market where direct investment is restricted. Which statement MOST accurately describes the risk profile of this arrangement?

options.A: The fund retains full market risk on the referenced equity and adds OTC counterparty risk on the swap itself
options.B: The equity swap eliminates market risk because the bank counterparty absorbs all price movements
options.C: The fund now has zero counterparty risk because it holds no securities directly
options.D: Equity swaps are exchange-traded so the clearing house eliminates counterparty risk

questions.explanation: An equity swap replicates the economic exposure of owning the referenced shares, so full market risk is retained. Because most equity swaps are OTC instruments, the fund also takes on counterparty risk to the swap dealer. Market risk is not eliminated by the swap structure. There is no central clearing house for most equity swaps, so counterparty risk is present, not zero.

questions.stem: An Asian option is embedded in a capital-protection structured note to determine the equity-linked payoff. Which characteristic makes this choice particularly suitable?

options.A: The Asian option can be exercised at any time before expiry, giving maximum flexibility
options.B: The Asian option has no expiry date, reducing the maturity mismatch risk
options.C: The Asian option's payoff is based on average prices over a period, reducing sensitivity to a single adverse end-date price
options.D: The Asian option is exchange-traded and therefore has tighter bid-offer spreads

questions.explanation: The Asian (average price) option computes the payoff from the average of the underlying price over a preset period rather than the price on one final date. This smoothing protects the investor against a sharp fall in the underlying on the maturity date alone, a key risk in point-in-time payoffs. The early-exercise feature describes an American option. The no-expiry description is false. Asian options are predominantly OTC, not exchange-traded.

questions.stem: Farhan holds a Bermuda-style option. On which dates can he exercise it?

options.B: Any trading day up to expiry
options.C: Never; Bermuda options are non-exercisable and settled by cash only at maturity
options.D: Only on a pre-set schedule of dates including the expiry date

questions.explanation: A Bermuda option is exercisable on a pre-determined set of dates that includes the expiry date, forming a hybrid between European (expiry only) and American (any day before expiry) styles. It is named by analogy with the island's location between Europe and America. Exercising only at expiry describes a European option. Exercising any day describes an American option.

questions.stem: Rajan holds four structured notes, all linked to Singapore property shares and all issued by the same European investment bank. He believes he has diversified his portfolio. What is the most significant risk he has overlooked?

options.A: He holds too many instruments and should consolidate into one note to reduce costs
options.B: His FX risk is excessive because all the underlying companies are in Singapore dollars
options.C: He has diversified market risk adequately by spreading across four different property names
options.D: He has concentrated both his sector market exposure and his issuer credit exposure, so a single event at the issuing bank collapses all four positions simultaneously

questions.explanation: Four notes linked to the same sector means undiversified sector market risk. All four issued by the same bank means that a default at the bank ends all four positions regardless of the underlying property performance. True diversification requires varying both the underlying and the issuer. Fewer notes with the same issuer creates the same problem, not a better one.

questions.stem: A retail ILP sub-fund has NAV of S$40,000,000. The fund holds S$2,800,000 of bonds issued by a single unrated corporate entity and S$1,800,000 of a rated investment-grade bank. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both positions are within limits; the single-entity cap is 10% for all issuers
options.B: The unrated corporate holding breaches its concentration limit of 5% of NAV
options.C: The rated bank holding breaches its limit because rated entities are capped at 5%
options.D: Neither position breaches any limit because the fund manager has full discretion

questions.explanation: For unrated and non-investment-grade corporate debt, the single-entity cap is reduced to 5% of NAV = 5% x 40,000,000 = S$2,000,000. The S$2,800,000 holding exceeds this. The rated bank holding of S$1,800,000 is within the standard 10% cap of S$4,000,000. The 5% cap applies to unrated entities specifically, not to rated ones. Fund manager discretion does not override MAS Code concentration rules.

questions.stem: A policy owner receives her structured ILP policy document and decides to cancel on Day 10. She paid a S$100,000 single premium and 100,000 units were allocated at S$1.0000. At the time of cancellation the unit price has fallen to S$0.9650. How much refund does she receive under the free-look right?
questions.explanation: The 14-day free-look refund equals the premium paid adjusted downward for any fall in unit NAV. Units = 100,000 / S$1.0000 = 100,000 units. Refund = 100,000 x S$0.9650 = S$96,500. The adjustment runs one way only: declines reduce the refund, but gains do not increase it beyond the original premium. The S$100,000 ignores the fall in unit price. The S$103,500 and S$101,000 figures both incorrectly pay out above the premium.

questions.stem: A Product Highlights Sheet for a structured ILP sub-fund contains 5 pages of body text, 2 pages of diagrams, a 1-page glossary, and a half-page disclaimer. Which rules has the insurer breached?

options.A: The body text exceeds the 4-page limit, the total including diagrams exceeds 8 pages, and disclaimers must not appear in a PHS
options.B: The font must be 12-point Times New Roman; only the font rule is breached
options.C: The glossary must not exceed half a page; only the glossary rule is breached
options.D: No rules are breached; the 8-page limit applies only to diagrams

questions.explanation: Under Notice MAS 307: body text (excluding diagrams and glossary) must not exceed 4 pages (this PHS has 5, breaching it); the total including diagrams and glossary must not exceed 8 pages (5 + 2 + 1 + 0.5 = 8.5 pages, breaching it); and an insurer shall refrain from including disclaimers in a PHS at all. The required minimum font is 10-point Times New Roman, not 12-point.

questions.stem: Which set of after-sales reporting timelines for a structured ILP sub-fund correctly matches the Notice MAS 307 requirements?
