options.A: Statement within 14 days of anniversary; Semi-Annual Report within 1 month; Audit Report within 2 months
options.B: Statement within 60 days of anniversary; Semi-Annual Report within 2 months; Audit Report within 3 months
options.C: Statement within 30 days of anniversary; Semi-Annual Report within 3 months; Audit Report within 6 months
options.D: Statement within 30 days of anniversary; Semi-Annual Report within 2 months; Audit Report within 3 months

questions.explanation: Notice MAS 307 requires: Statement to Policy Owners within 30 days after each policy anniversary; Semi-Annual Report within 2 months of the period end; Relevant Audit Report within 3 months of the period end. The 14-day figure confuses the free-look period with the reporting deadline. The 6-month audit deadline has no basis in the rules. The 60-day statement deadline is too long.

questions.stem: A client asks whether a portfolio bond will pay him a fixed coupon like the Singapore Savings Bond he already holds. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: Yes; portfolio bonds pay a fixed coupon from the bond component of the structure
options.B: No; any regular payment from a portfolio bond is funded by redeeming units, permanently reducing the capital base
options.C: Yes; portfolio bonds are covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme so the coupon is guaranteed
options.D: No; portfolio bonds pay a variable coupon linked to an interest rate index

questions.explanation: A portfolio bond is not a bond. Any income drawn from it is generated by selling (redeeming) units, which reduces the number of units held and permanently erodes the capital base. There is no coupon, no par repayment, and no principal protection. Portfolio bonds are not covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme. The value tracks underlying investments, not an interest rate index.

questions.stem: Wei Ling's portfolio bond started with S$160,000 in an equity fund and S$160,000 in a bond fund. Three years later the equity fund is worth S$206,000 and the bond fund is worth S$114,000. She rebalances to the original 50/50 split. How much moves from the equity fund to the bond fund?
questions.explanation: Total portfolio = 206,000 + 114,000 = S$320,000. Each side needs 320,000 / 2 = S$160,000. The equity fund holds S$206,000, which is S$46,000 above its target. That S$46,000 transfers to the bond fund. This illustrates the opportunity cost of rebalancing: units are sold from the outperformer to restore the risk profile. The S$52,000 uses an incorrect total. The S$26,000 halves the required transfer by mistake.

questions.stem: The corn cash price in Farmerville is S$3.10 per bushel and the July futures price is S$3.55 per bushel. The historically expected basis for this delivery month is -S$0.50. Which statement correctly describes the current basis and its strength?

options.A: Basis = +S$0.45; the market is in backwardation
options.B: Basis = -S$0.50; the basis is exactly at expectation
options.C: Basis = -S$0.45; the basis is narrow/strong because cash is closer to futures than expected
options.D: Basis = -S$0.45; the basis is wide/weak because cash is farther from futures than expected

questions.explanation: Basis = spot - futures = 3.10 - 3.55 = -S$0.45. The expected basis is -S$0.50. The observed basis (-S$0.45) is less negative than expected, meaning cash is closer to the futures price than usual. This is a narrow or strong basis. A positive basis would mean cash is above futures, which is not the case. The wide/weak description applies when cash is farther from futures than expected, i.e. more negative than -S$0.50.

questions.stem: Ng, aged 45, wants to invest S$120,000 for 18 months before using the funds for a property down payment. An adviser recommends a structured ILP with a 5% front-end charge and a 1.8% annual fund management fee. Which statement about suitability is most accurate?

options.A: The product is suitable if Ng has a medium risk tolerance
options.B: The product is suitable once Ng reads the Product Highlights Sheet
options.C: The product is suitable because the 5% charge is refunded if held to maturity
options.D: The product is likely unsuitable; the 18-month horizon is too short for the fee drag to be recovered and Ng has a specific known liquidity need

questions.explanation: Structured ILPs are explicitly unsuitable for short-term investors. First-year costs can reach around 8% of the single premium, requiring the fund to earn that amount just to break even. Over 18 months, recovery is unlikely. A known liquidity event in 18 months compounds the mismatch further. The front-end charge is not refunded at maturity. Risk tolerance is secondary to the fundamental horizon and liquidity mismatch.

questions.stem: In the SIP case study, which scenario produces the HIGHEST total cash payout to the policy owner over the full five-year term on a S$10,000 single premium, and why is this counter-intuitive?

options.A: All six stocks remain below 92% for all five years; because the guaranteed 4% floor applies throughout
options.B: All six stocks rise strongly to 108% in month three, triggering early redemption; because the trigger produces a bonus payment
options.C: The six stocks fluctuate with at least one below 92% on every trading day; because mixed performance generates the highest average payout
options.D: All six stocks consistently stay between 92% and 108% throughout all five years; because this moderate performance triggers the maximum 20% payout for the full five-year term

questions.explanation: The moderate scenario (stocks range-bound 92-108%, n=N all five years) pays 20% per year: S$10,000 principal + S$10,000 in payouts = S$20,000 total. The counter-intuitive result is that the BEST stock performance scenario (early redemption after 3 months) pays only S$10,000 + S$480 = S$10,480, the lowest total. The guaranteed-floor scenarios (all below 92%, or mixed) pay S$12,000. The 20% annual cap means stocks staying well-behaved inside the 92-108% band for all five years is the best outcome for the investor, not the strongest rally.

questions.stem: Mdm Koh, age 58, is retiring in 2 years. She has S$80,000 to invest and tells her adviser she needs the money back in full no later than her retirement date. Her risk appetite is low. The adviser is considering a 3-year capital-protection structured note whose principal is returned only at maturity. Which statement about this recommendation is most accurate?

options.A: The product is unsuitable because the 3-year maturity extends beyond Mdm Koh's 2-year horizon; if she exits early she faces a mark-to-market loss and the capital-protection feature has not yet arrived
options.B: The product is suitable because a capital-protection feature eliminates all risk regardless of when she exits
options.C: The product is suitable because her low risk appetite matches the capital-protection objective of the note
options.D: The product is unsuitable because structured notes always generate losses in falling markets

questions.explanation: Capital protection in a structured note applies only at maturity. A client who must exit before maturity receives the mark-to-market value, which can be below par if yields have risen or the option has lost value. Mdm Koh's 2-year horizon is shorter than the 3-year maturity, so early redemption is likely and the protection never arrives. Her low risk appetite makes this mismatch decisive. The 'suitable because capital-protection eliminates all risk' option ignores that the protection is time-conditional.

questions.stem: Mr Raj invests S$10,000 in a 5-year structured note. The zero-coupon bond portion costs S$8,000 at issue and will grow to S$10,000 at maturity. The remaining S$2,000 buys a call option on an index. At maturity the index has risen 30% and the option strike is at-the-money at inception. The option premium was 14% of notional. What is the participation rate and the total maturity payout? (Assume: participation rate = derivative budget / premium cost of the option.)

options.C: Participation rate approximately 142.9%; payout approximately S$14,286

questions.explanation: Option budget = S$2,000. Option premium amount = 14% x S$10,000 = S$1,400. Participation rate = 2,000 / 1,400 = 142.86%. Index rose 30%, so participation gain = S$10,000 x 1.4286 x 0.30 = S$4,286. Total payout = S$10,000 (from bond) + S$4,286 = S$14,286. The '100% participation; S$13,000' option ignores that the budget exceeds the premium cost, giving a rate above 100%.

questions.stem: Ms Chen, age 42, holds a structured ILP she purchased 18 months ago with a S$50,000 single premium. She paid a 5% front-end charge. The sub-fund has since gained 3%. Her adviser correctly tells her that her current surrender value is approximately S$48,825. All of the following statements about her position are correct EXCEPT:

options.A: Her S$50,000 premium was reduced by 5% to S$47,500 invested in the sub-fund on day one
options.B: The sub-fund then grew by 3%, bringing the value to approximately S$47,500 x 1.03 = S$48,925, before annual fund charges are deducted
options.C: The surrender value equals the market value of her units; there is no guaranteed surrender floor
options.D: She is below her original S$50,000 premium because the front-end charge plus fund management fees have not yet been recovered by the 3% sub-fund gain

questions.explanation: The raw sub-fund gain gives S$47,500 x 1.03 = S$48,925 before annual fund charges. Once the ongoing management charge is deducted over 18 months, the net surrender value falls to the stated S$48,825, so the S$48,925 figure is the one statement that stops short of the full deduction and is incorrect. The rest are accurate: the 5% front-end charge is deducted first, the surrender value floats with NAV with no guaranteed floor, and the net position sits below the S$50,000 premium.

questions.stem: Encik Hassan, age 35, earns S$120,000 a year and has a 25-year investment horizon. He is considering either a portfolio bond or a standard structured ILP. He wants to appoint his own preferred external fund managers and hold a mix of equities, bonds and derivatives within one policy. Which product better fits this requirement, and why?

options.A: Standard structured ILP, because it allows unlimited fund manager appointments
options.B: Standard structured ILP, because it gives the owner full trading discretion over individual securities
options.C: Portfolio bond, because it also gives guaranteed capital protection at all times
options.D: Portfolio bond, because it lets the owner appoint managers within the insurer's platform and access equities, bonds, derivatives and CIS, which a standard ILP does not permit

questions.explanation: A standard ILP restricts the owner to the insurer's own funds with no say over fund manager selection. A portfolio bond goes a step further, allowing the owner to appoint managers of their choice within the insurer's platform and access cash, equities, bonds, derivatives and CIS. Encik Hassan's requirement for external manager appointments is the decisive feature. Portfolio bonds do not provide guaranteed capital protection, so that distractor is wrong.

questions.stem: A reverse convertible note is linked to a Singapore-listed bank stock currently at S$28.00. The kick-in level is set at 75% of the current price and the note pays a 10% coupon. At maturity the stock is at S$18.00. The note specifies delivery of 3,571 shares per S$100,000 par if kick-in is breached. What does the investor receive per S$100,000 par, and what is the percentage loss?

options.A: 3,571 shares x S$18.00 = S$64,278 plus S$10,000 coupon = S$74,278; a loss of approximately 25.7%
options.B: Par S$100,000 plus coupon S$10,000; a gain of 10%
options.C: 3,571 shares x S$21.00 = S$74,991 plus coupon; kick-in was not breached
options.D: S$100,000 par only; coupon is forfeited on breach

questions.explanation: Kick-in level = 75% x S$28.00 = S$21.00. The stock closed at S$18.00, which is below S$21.00, so the kick-in is breached. The investor receives 3,571 x S$18.00 = S$64,278 plus the S$10,000 coupon = S$74,278. Loss = (100,000 - 74,278) / 100,000 = 25.7%. The 'par plus coupon; 10% gain' option would only apply if the stock stayed above S$21.00 at maturity, which it did not.

questions.stem: A client holds 10,000 units in ILP Sub-fund A with a bid price of S$1.2000 and an offer price of S$1.2600. She instructs a chargeable switch into Sub-fund B, which has a bid price of S$0.9500 and an offer price of S$1.0000. There is no explicit switching fee, but the switch is executed bid-to-offer. How many units of Sub-fund B does she receive?
questions.explanation: She sells Sub-fund A at the bid: 10,000 x S$1.2000 = S$12,000 proceeds. She buys Sub-fund B at the offer: S$12,000 / S$1.0000 = 12,000 units. On a bid-to-offer switch the sale proceeds are divided by the destination fund's offer price. The '11,368 units' distractor would arise from incorrectly dividing by S$1.0560 (an average). The '9,500 units' distractor uses the bid price of Sub-fund B incorrectly as the purchase price.

questions.stem: During a structured ILP sales process, which of the following is the CORRECT sequence of document delivery and the consumer action that the free-look period enables?

options.A: Policy document is issued first; client can cancel within 7 days for a guaranteed full premium refund with no adjustments
options.B: Product Highlights Sheet is issued only after purchase; client cannot cancel once invested
options.C: Product Summary and Benefit Illustration must be provided during the sales process; the PHS at the point of sale; the policy document is issued after purchase and triggers a 14-day free-look during which cancellation entitles a refund subject to market value adjustment on invested units
options.D: The Audited Report is issued during the sales process; free-look is 30 days

questions.explanation: The Product Summary, Benefit Illustration and Product Highlights Sheet are all pre-purchase documents. The policy document is issued after purchase and starts the 14-day free-look. Cancellation within the free-look gives a refund adjusted for any downward market movement in the unit price, so the refund may be less than the premium paid if units have fallen. The '7-day period with guaranteed full refund' option understates the period and ignores the market value adjustment.

questions.stem: Mr Tan invests S$200,000 in a portfolio bond carrying: product charge 0.70% per year, average fund charge 1.30% per year, mortality charge 0.15% per year, and a one-off surrender charge of 3% if surrendered within 5 years. His adviser says the annual tax saving inside the insurance wrapper is approximately S$2,800 per year. In year one, does the cost of ownership exceed the tax benefit?

options.A: No, because the mortality charge offsets the tax saving exactly
options.B: No, because fund charges are paid by the fund, not the investor
options.C: Yes, because the surrender charge alone exceeds the tax saving
options.D: Yes, because annual recurring charges total 0.70% + 1.30% + 0.15% = 2.15% x S$200,000 = S$4,300 per year, which exceeds the S$2,800 tax saving

questions.explanation: Total recurring annual charge = (0.70 + 1.30 + 0.15)% = 2.15% x S$200,000 = S$4,300. That exceeds the S$2,800 annual tax saving by S$1,500, so the cost outweighs the benefit in year one. The surrender charge is a one-off exit cost and does not affect this annual comparison. The portfolio bond study text specifically warns that the tax benefit can be outweighed by the cost of ownership.

questions.stem: Mdm Lim, age 61, retired last year. She wants a product that provides regular income and also preserves capital for her estate. Her adviser recommends a portfolio bond with monthly unit redemptions to generate income. Which risk must the adviser MOST prominently disclose?

options.A: That the portfolio bond is covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme up to S$75,000
options.B: That issuer credit risk is eliminated because assets are held by a trustee
options.C: That the mortality charge increases with age and may consume a significant portion of her portfolio in later years
options.D: That regular income from a portfolio bond is funded by redeeming units, so a falling market permanently reduces the capital base, and capital protection is not provided

questions.explanation: Regular income from a portfolio bond is funded by redeeming (selling) units. In a falling market this means Mdm Lim continuously liquidates units at depressed prices, permanently reducing the capital base. Portfolio bonds do not protect capital. This is the risk most relevant to a retired client seeking both income and capital preservation. The 'DIS coverage' option is false: ILP wrappers are not deposits. The 'trustee holds assets' option describes a CIS structure; in an ILP the insurer is the legal owner in a quasi-trust arrangement.

questions.stem: Under the Superior Income Plan (SIP) case study, on a S$10,000 single premium policy: in Scenario 1 (best market performance, early redemption at 3 months, 60 trading days elapsed out of 250), what is the exact annual payout received, and what is the total cash received when the policy terminates?

options.A: Non-guaranteed payout = 20% x 60/250 = 4.8% x S$10,000 = S$480; total received = S$10,480
options.B: Non-guaranteed payout = 20% x 60/250 = 4.8%; guaranteed applies instead at 4% = S$400; total = S$10,400

questions.explanation: Non-guaranteed payout = 20% x 60/250 = 4.8%. Since 4.8% > 4% guaranteed, the payout is S$10,000 x 4.8% = S$480. At early redemption the single premium is also returned, so total = S$10,000 + S$480 = S$10,480. The policy terminates after three months. The 'guaranteed 4% applies instead' option is wrong because 4.8% > 4%, so the non-guaranteed figure is the higher one and applies.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a structured fund from a structured ILP in terms of who bears issuer default risk?

options.A: Both are equally exposed to issuer default because both are unsecured debentures
options.B: A structured ILP exposes the owner to issuer default, but a structured fund eliminates it entirely since assets are exchange-traded
options.C: A structured fund holds assets through a third-party custodian (trustee), so investors are not exposed to the fund issuer's insolvency; a structured ILP is an insurance policy where the insurer is the legal owner in a quasi-trust, giving a different but not eliminated credit exposure
options.D: There is no difference; both are covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme

questions.explanation: In a structured fund (CIS trust structure) the trustee holds the assets for investors, so fund manager insolvency does not put investor assets at risk. In a structured ILP the insurer is the legal owner in a quasi-trust under the Insurance Act, not a true trust, giving a different legal position. Neither is covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme. The 'both are unsecured debentures' description applies to structured notes, not funds or ILPs.

questions.stem: Ms Priya, age 29, wants to invest S$30,000 for 10 years in a regular-premium ILP. Her adviser quotes a plan where 50% of year-1 premiums are allocated (i.e. 50% front-loaded charge applies in year 1). Her annual premium is S$3,600. How many units does she receive in year 1 if the offer price is S$1.00 and the allocation rate is 50%?
questions.explanation: Allocated premium in year 1 = S$3,600 x 50% = S$1,800. Units received = S$1,800 / S$1.00 = 1,800 units. The '3,600 units' option ignores the front-load and assumes full allocation. The '1,440 units' option would arise from a 40% allocation rate, not 50%. The '2,880 units' option would arise from an 80% rate. The factbank notes that for regular-premium plans the front-end allocation rate can be as low as 20-50% in year 1, making the first-year cost extremely high.

questions.stem: An adviser is reviewing two products for Mr Lim, age 50, who has a 7-year horizon and moderate risk appetite. Product X is a structured note with capital protection at maturity in year 7. Product Y is a structured ILP with no capital guarantee but a diversified sub-fund and 5% front-end charge. Mr Lim mentions he may need some of the funds in year 4 for his child's university fees. Which statement correctly identifies the suitability issue with Product X?

options.A: Product X is unsuitable because structured notes carry no market risk
options.B: Product X is unsuitable because the front-end charge exceeds 10%
options.C: Product X is unsuitable because its capital protection applies only at maturity in year 7; if Mr Lim exits in year 4 for university fees, he receives the mark-to-market value with no capital protection, potentially below his investment
options.D: Product X is unsuitable because structured notes are not permitted to be sold to clients aged over 45

questions.explanation: Product X protects capital only at maturity in year 7. If Mr Lim exits in year 4 to fund university fees, he receives the mark-to-market value of the structured note, which reflects current rates and option time value and may be below par. The capital-protection feature has not matured. The horizon mismatch between his 7-year product and his year-4 liquidity need is the decisive suitability failure. Front-end charges on structured notes are typically embedded in pricing rather than explicit, so the 10% option is not the right concept here.

questions.stem: The Product Highlights Sheet (PHS) for a structured ILP sub-fund contains a disclaimer paragraph and runs to 5 pages of text plus 4 pages of charts. Which rule violations has the insurer committed?

options.A: Two violations: the PHS must carry no disclaimers, and text must not exceed 4 pages (total including diagrams must not exceed 8 pages, and here text alone is 5 pages, breaching both limits)
options.B: One violation: the disclaimer is permitted but the 5-page text breaches the limit
options.C: No violations: 9 pages total is within the 10-page limit
options.D: One violation: the PHS must use 12-point Arial, not 10-point Times New Roman

questions.explanation: PHS rules under Notice MAS 307 state: no disclaimers permitted, text (excluding diagrams and glossary) must not exceed 4 pages, and total including diagrams must not exceed 8 pages. Here the text runs 5 pages (breaches the 4-page limit) and the total is 9 pages (breaches the 8-page ceiling). The disclaimer is never permitted in a PHS. The font rule is 10-point Times New Roman, not 12-point Arial.

questions.stem: Encik Farid, age 46, holds a portfolio bond. His original allocation was 60% equity fund and 40% bond fund on a S$250,000 investment. Three years later the equity fund has grown to S$172,500 and the bond fund to S$87,500, a total of S$260,000. He instructs a rebalance back to 60/40. How much must move from the equity fund to the bond fund?
questions.explanation: Target allocation: 60% x S$260,000 = S$156,000 in equity; 40% x S$260,000 = S$104,000 in bond. Current equity = S$172,500; current bond = S$87,500. Transfer needed from equity to bond = S$172,500 - S$156,000 = S$16,500. Verify: equity after = S$156,000, bond after = S$87,500 + S$16,500 = S$104,000. Total still S$260,000 and 60/40 split. The S$12,500 distractor uses the original S$250,000 total rather than the current S$260,000.

questions.stem: A structured note is marketed to a client by the distributor with the phrase 'your investment is fully capital protected at all times.' The note is a 5-year product with capital return only at maturity. Which TWO problems does this marketing phrase create?

options.A: It is accurate because capital protection notes always protect capital intraday
options.B: It misrepresents the product by implying protection exists before maturity, and it uses a phrase that has been banned in Singapore since September 2009 unless the product genuinely provides the capital protection at all times
options.C: The only problem is that 'capital protected' should be replaced with 'capital guaranteed'
options.D: It violates SGX listing rules but does not affect retail investors

questions.explanation: Two problems: first, the phrase 'capital protected at all times' is false because protection applies only at maturity, not during the 5-year term; exiting early means receiving a mark-to-market value. Second, since September 2009 MAS banned use of 'capital protected' or 'capital guaranteed' unless the product genuinely provides that protection as described. An intraday or at-all-times protection that does not exist is precisely the misleading label the ban addressed.

questions.stem: Ms Tan, age 38, has an existing portfolio of Singapore equities valued at S$800,000 with a portfolio beta of 1.35. She is worried about a near-term market correction but does not want to sell her holdings. The STI is at 3,200 and the June STI futures contract trades at 3,150 with a multiplier of S$10 per point. How many futures contracts should she short to hedge the portfolio?
questions.explanation: Price coverage per contract = 3,150 x S$10 = S$31,500. Raw ratio = S$800,000 / S$31,500 = 25.40 contracts. Adjusted for beta: 25.40 x 1.35 = 34.29, rounded to 34 contracts. The '28 contracts' distractor arises from using the STI spot (3,200) instead of the futures price (3,150) and rounding down. The '25 contracts' distractor ignores the beta entirely. Short-selling the futures contracts creates a position that offsets the portfolio's market sensitivity.

questions.stem: In the Choice Fund under Case 2 (Lifestyle Plan), the Secure Price is set at S$1.08 per unit at maturity. The per-unit NAV at maturity is S$0.97. What amount does the policy owner receive per unit at maturity, and why?

options.A: S$1.08 per unit, because the Secure Price is a guaranteed floor
options.B: S$0.97 per unit, because the Secure Price is a non-guaranteed target; if NAV is below the Secure Price at maturity, the policy owner receives the unit price, not the Secure Price
options.C: S$1.00 per unit, because the death benefit floor applies at maturity
options.D: S$0.97 per unit plus a top-up from XYZ Bank under the guarantee arrangement

questions.explanation: The Secure Price is a target the manager strives for, set yearly at the insurer's discretion. It is explicitly non-guaranteed. If the per-unit NAV is below the Secure Price at maturity, the policy owner receives the unit price (S$0.97), not the Secure Price. The 'guaranteed floor' option is the exact misconception the case study warns against: the Secure Price gives the impression of a floor but carries no legal commitment to pay it.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly matches each participation product to its defining feature?

options.A: Tracker mirrors the underlying one-for-one; bonus pays a bonus if a barrier is never breached; airbag cushions moderate falls before losses begin
options.B: Tracker caps the upside at a strike; bonus guarantees a fixed coupon; airbag doubles the downside exposure
options.C: Tracker pays a fixed coupon; bonus mirrors the underlying one-for-one; airbag knocks out on any rise
options.D: Tracker cushions moderate falls; bonus mirrors the underlying; airbag pays a bonus at a barrier

questions.explanation: Participation products aim to take part in the underlying's performance. A tracker certificate follows it one-for-one, a bonus certificate pays a bonus provided the barrier is never touched, and an airbag certificate absorbs a moderate fall before the investor starts to lose. The other pairings shuffle the three designs.

questions.stem: Mdm Wong, age 52, instructs her adviser she wants 'income from her investment.' Her adviser recommends a portfolio bond and sets up monthly unit redemptions of S$1,500 from a S$300,000 portfolio bond. The portfolio drops 15% in the first year. Which statement about Mdm Wong's position at year-end is most accurate?

options.A: She has received S$18,000 income and her portfolio remains at S$300,000 because the bond guarantees capital
options.B: She has received S$18,000 in cash from unit redemptions; her remaining portfolio value is approximately S$300,000 x 0.85 - S$18,000 = S$237,000, and there is no capital guarantee
options.C: She has received S$18,000 income; her portfolio has risen to S$300,000 x 1.15 = S$345,000 because the bond protected her from losses
options.D: She has received only S$9,000 because redemptions are capped at 3% per year

questions.explanation: A portfolio bond does not protect capital. Monthly redemptions of S$1,500 x 12 = S$18,000 are withdrawals funded by selling units. The remaining portfolio before redemptions at year-end = S$300,000 x 0.85 = S$255,000. After the S$18,000 redeemed during the year, the residual is approximately S$255,000 - S$18,000 = S$237,000. In a falling market she is selling units at depressed prices and permanently eroding her capital base. No portfolio bond guarantee exists.

questions.stem: Which statement about the valuation and liquidity rules for a structured ILP sub-fund is CORRECT?

options.A: The sub-fund must be valued at least weekly, and redemptions can never be restricted
options.B: The sub-fund must be valued at least annually, with redemptions suspended at the insurer's discretion
options.C: The sub-fund must be valued at least monthly, and a redemption cap of around 10% may be imposed to protect remaining holders
options.D: Valuation frequency is left entirely to the fund manager as long as it is disclosed

questions.explanation: A structured ILP sub-fund must be valued at least monthly, and the fund may cap redemptions at around 10% to protect the remaining policy owners from forced sales. Weekly valuation is not required, and the monthly minimum is a regulatory floor rather than a manager's free choice.

questions.stem: An ILP sub-fund has NAV of S$40,000,000. An investment manager wants to buy bonds issued by Alpha Corp, a single entity with no credit rating. What is the maximum amount the fund may invest in Alpha Corp's bonds under the MAS concentration rules?

options.A: S$2,000,000, because unrated single-entity exposure is capped at 5% of NAV
options.B: S$4,000,000, because the 10% single-entity limit applies
options.C: S$8,000,000, because the 20% group limit applies
options.D: S$14,000,000, because Alpha Corp qualifies for the 35% government issuer ceiling

questions.explanation: Under the ILP sub-fund concentration rules, the single-entity limit is normally 10% of NAV (S$4,000,000). However, if the entity's paper is unrated or non-investment grade, the ceiling drops to 5% of NAV. Alpha Corp has no credit rating, so the tighter 5% limit applies: 5% x S$40,000,000 = S$2,000,000. The 10% general limit applies only to rated entities. The 35% ceiling is reserved for government or supranational issuers, which Alpha Corp is not.

questions.stem: Mr Ng, age 44, holds a structured ILP with a single premium of S$100,000 invested 3 years ago. The sub-fund has delivered a cumulative net return of 4% after all charges. He surrenders today. Assuming no surrender penalty and single (bid-only) pricing at NAV, what surrender value does he receive?

options.A: S$100,000 because the policy guarantees return of premium after 3 years
options.B: S$104,000 less the 5% initial charge already taken = S$98,800
options.C: S$104,000 because the 4% cumulative return is added to the original premium
options.D: S$95,000 x 1.04 = S$98,800, because the 5% front-end charge was deducted on day one, giving S$95,000 invested, which grew 4% to S$98,800

questions.explanation: The surrender value of a structured ILP equals the current market value of units held, which is NAV. The question states the sub-fund has delivered a cumulative net return of 4% after all charges on the original S$100,000 investment. Net return of 4% on S$100,000 gives a current value of S$104,000. There is no guaranteed surrender floor, but the 4% net gain means the value exceeds the original premium. The S$95,000 x 1.04 working misapplies the 4% to the post-charge invested amount; the question states net return on the original premium.

questions.stem: A client in a high-tax bracket wants to invest S$500,000 for 15 years. Her adviser shortlists: (i) a direct portfolio of unit trusts, and (ii) a portfolio bond. She invests in only two funds and does not plan to change fund managers. Which statement gives the strongest reason to prefer the direct unit trust portfolio over the portfolio bond?

options.A: The unit trust portfolio is covered by the Policy Owners' Protection Scheme but the portfolio bond is not
options.B: The direct unit trust portfolio avoids the additional layer of charges (product charge, mortality charge, surrender charge) that the portfolio bond stacks on top of the fund charges, and given she uses only two funds the flexibility premium is not justified
options.C: The unit trust portfolio allows her to appoint external fund managers, unlike the portfolio bond
options.D: The direct unit trust portfolio provides a capital guarantee that the portfolio bond does not

questions.explanation: The study text identifies three client types for whom portfolio bonds are unsuitable: those seeking insurance protection, those with short horizons, and those who do not need the flexibility because they hold only one or two funds. This client fits the third category. The portfolio bond stacks product charge, mortality charge, surrender charge and other fees on top of fund charges. If she uses only two funds and does not need the flexibility, the additional costs outweigh the benefits. Unit trusts do not provide a capital guarantee, so the guarantee claim is false.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes an interest rate swap from a currency swap?

options.A: An interest rate swap exchanges full principal at the start and end, while a currency swap nets its payments
options.B: In an interest rate swap the same-currency payments are netted, while a currency swap exchanges both principal and interest in full with no netting
options.C: Both types of swap net their payments because they are traded on an exchange
options.D: A currency swap involves only one currency, while an interest rate swap involves two

questions.explanation: Both legs of an interest rate swap are in the same currency, so only the difference changes hands. A currency swap involves two currencies, so principal and interest are exchanged in full and nothing is netted. Swaps are over-the-counter contracts, not exchange-traded.

questions.stem: Mr Ahmad, age 55, has S$150,000 in a portfolio bond that he is considering surrendering to fund a property purchase. The surrender charge is 2.5% in year 5. The current portfolio value is S$158,000. He also faces a valuation charge of S$50 for requesting a special paper statement. What is his net surrender proceeds?

options.B: S$158,000 x (1 - 0.025) = S$154,050; then S$154,050 - S$50 valuation charge = S$154,000 net proceeds
options.C: S$158,000 with no deductions because surrender charges are illegal in Singapore
options.D: S$150,000 because the portfolio bond guarantees a minimum return of capital

questions.explanation: Surrender charge = 2.5% x S$158,000 = S$3,950. Value after surrender charge = S$158,000 - S$3,950 = S$154,050. Valuation charge for the special paper statement = S$50. Net surrender proceeds = S$154,050 - S$50 = S$154,000. Portfolio bonds do not guarantee return of capital; the S$150,000 option wrongly implies a capital guarantee. Surrender charges are a standard feature of portfolio bonds, not illegal.

questions.stem: A client asks her adviser whether a structured deposit she is considering is covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme (DIS). Her current savings account is covered. The adviser correctly responds:

options.A: Yes, all bank products marketed as deposits are covered by the DIS
options.B: No, structured deposits are specifically excluded from the DIS even though they carry the word 'deposit' in their name; only ordinary deposits are covered
options.C: Yes, but only up to S$25,000 rather than the standard limit
options.D: No, but a structured deposit is instead covered by the Policy Owners' Protection Scheme

questions.explanation: Structured deposits are excluded from the Deposit Insurance Scheme in Singapore. The word 'deposit' in the product name does not confer the same protection as an ordinary bank deposit. Only ordinary deposits (savings, current, fixed deposits) from DIS-scheme members are covered. The Policy Owners' Protection Scheme covers insurance policy owners, not structured deposit holders.

questions.stem: In a structured product with barrier features, what happens when a kick-in barrier is touched?

options.A: The product's upside is immediately locked in for the investor
options.B: The product converts into an ordinary bank deposit
options.C: The coupon steps up to compensate the investor for the breach
options.D: The investor becomes exposed to downside losses that did not apply before the barrier was touched

questions.explanation: A kick-in barrier changes the payoff once touched: downside exposure that was previously shielded suddenly applies to the investor. A knock-out barrier does the opposite job, terminating the upside. These discontinuous triggers are a defining structural risk of barrier products.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes how the SIP guarantee from XYZ Bank differs from ABC Insurance's own obligation, and what happens to the guarantee if XYZ is liquidated?

options.A: ABC provides the guarantee directly; XYZ liquidation has no effect
options.B: XYZ provides a secondary guarantee; ABC's primary obligation always remains intact
options.C: MAS stands behind both ABC and XYZ jointly
options.D: XYZ Bank provides the guarantee for the 4% minimum payout and principal repayment; the policy document states the guarantee terminates if XYZ goes into liquidation, so counterparty risk sits with XYZ; without that clause ABC as primary party would have had to honour it

questions.explanation: The policy document explicitly identifies XYZ Bank as the guarantor and states the guarantee ends if XYZ goes into liquidation. This clause shifts the counterparty risk from ABC to XYZ, and by extension to the policy owner. Without that clause, ABC as the primary insurance contract party would have been obligated to pay even if XYZ failed. The policy owner must therefore assess XYZ's credit quality, not just ABC's.

questions.stem: Ms Ho, age 48, has a 12-year horizon and moderate-to-high risk appetite. She wants the flexibility to shift between equities, fixed income and alternatives as her views change over the years, using one insurance-wrapper policy. She also needs a consolidated annual statement. Which product is most appropriate, and what is the key charge she should watch?

options.A: A standard structured ILP, because it offers the widest fund choice with no surrender charges
options.B: A portfolio bond, because it provides the required multi-asset flexibility, external fund manager access, and consolidated reporting; she should watch the stacked annual charges that include product charge, fund charges, mortality charge and potentially surrender charge
options.C: A structured note, because it has the lowest fees and greatest flexibility
options.D: A term deposit, because it is the safest product for a 12-year horizon

questions.explanation: Ms Ho's requirements, multi-asset access, ability to change allocation over time, external managers, and consolidated reporting, match a portfolio bond precisely. A standard ILP limits her to the insurer's own sub-funds. A structured note has a fixed payoff profile with no flexibility. The key charge risk for a portfolio bond is the stack of product charge, fund charges, mortality charge, and potentially surrender charge and valuation charge, all deducted from her investment. A 12-year horizon gives time to recover those costs.

questions.stem: The Marketing Manager of an insurer wants to include in the Product Summary for a new sub-fund: (i) a comparison of the sub-fund's 3-year simulated performance against a rival equity fund, and (ii) a projection that the fund is 'likely to deliver 6% per annum.' Which of these is/are prohibited?

options.A: Both are prohibited: simulated past performance may not be included in any document given to policy owners, and insurers shall not predict future or likely performance
options.B: Only the 6% projection is prohibited; simulated performance comparisons are permitted in the Product Summary
options.C: Neither is prohibited if accompanied by a risk warning
options.D: Only the competitor comparison is prohibited; projections are permitted if clearly labelled as estimates

questions.explanation: MAS rules on structured ILP Product Summaries prohibit three things: predictions of future or likely performance, simulated or back-tested track records, and comparisons with another fund unless they share a similar risk profile and figures are net of fees. The simulated comparison is specifically banned regardless of the risk warning, and the 6% projection is exactly the future performance prediction the rules forbid. Both items are prohibited.

questions.stem: Mr Loh, age 62, retires next month. He holds a structured ILP he purchased 4 years ago. The sub-fund has dropped 8% over the 4-year period. His adviser recommends he switch from the current growth sub-fund into a capital-protected sub-fund within the same ILP. The switching fee is 1% of the value being switched. The current value is S$92,000. What amount will actually be invested in the capital-protected sub-fund?
questions.explanation: Switching fee = 1% x S$92,000 = S$920. Amount invested in the new sub-fund = S$92,000 - S$920 = S$91,080. Switching is done on a bid-offer basis which is equivalent here to deducting the switching fee. The S$92,000 option ignores the switching fee. Note that even after switching to a capital-protected sub-fund, the protection applies only at the maturity date of that sub-fund, not on the day of the switch. The adviser should disclose this.

questions.stem: A fund manager running a S$30,000,000 ILP sub-fund enters an OTC interest rate swap with Dealer X, which is a financial institution supervised by a recognised regulator. The mark-to-market exposure is currently S$3,200,000. The dealer posts S$800,000 of eligible collateral. What is the effective exposure after collateral, and does it breach the 10% single-entity OTC limit?

options.A: Effective exposure S$4,000,000; breaches the S$3,000,000 limit
options.B: Effective exposure S$3,200,000; does not breach because OTC limits do not apply to swaps
options.C: Effective exposure S$3,200,000; breaches the 10% limit of S$3,000,000
options.D: Effective exposure S$2,400,000; does not breach the 10% limit of S$3,000,000 after collateral

questions.explanation: 10% single-entity limit = 10% x S$30,000,000 = S$3,000,000. Mark-to-market exposure = S$3,200,000. Collateral posted = S$800,000. Effective exposure after collateral = S$3,200,000 - S$800,000 = S$2,400,000. S$2,400,000 < S$3,000,000, so no breach. Collateral reduces the counted exposure, which is how a fund can hold a position that would otherwise breach the cap. The 'no limit applies to swaps' option is incorrect: OTC derivative exposures count toward single-entity limits.

questions.stem: Encik Zulkifli, age 33, has S$20,000 to invest and an investment horizon of 20 years. He has a high risk appetite and wants maximum capital growth with no income needs. He has no existing structured products. His adviser shortlists a tracker certificate and a capital-protection structured note. Which is more suitable, and why?

options.A: The capital-protection note, because it guarantees a minimum return regardless of market direction
options.B: The tracker certificate, because with a 20-year horizon and high risk appetite he can take the full upside exposure with no participation cap; a capital-protection note would sacrifice upside for protection he does not need at his age and risk level
options.C: The capital-protection note, because tracker certificates have no maturity date and cannot be held
options.D: Neither; both products are only suitable for clients aged over 50

questions.explanation: A tracker certificate mirrors the underlying one-for-one with no upside cap and no downside protection. For Encik Zulkifli, 33 years old with a 20-year horizon, high risk appetite, no income need, and capital growth as the sole objective, the full market participation of a tracker certificate fits his profile. A capital-protection note sacrifices upside participation to fund the protection, which is unnecessary and reduces expected return for a client who does not need the safety net. Tracker certificates may have no maturity date, making them suitable for long-term holding.

questions.stem: The Statement to Policy Owners for a structured ILP must be sent within how many days of the policy anniversary, and what must it show about mortality and administration charges?

options.A: Within 30 days of the policy anniversary; it must show fees and charges payable through deduction of premium or deduction of units, identified by purpose such as initial charge, insurance coverage charge and switching fee
options.B: Within 60 days; mortality charges need not be itemised
options.C: Within 14 days; only investment returns need be shown
options.D: Within 2 months; charges are summarised as a single annual figure

questions.explanation: The Statement to Policy Owners must be sent within 30 days after each policy anniversary. It must show, among other items, fees and charges payable through deduction of premium or deduction of units, identified by purpose: this means initial charges, insurance coverage charges (mortality and administration) and switching fees are each separately identified. The '60 days / charges not itemised' option confuses the statement timeline with the Semi-Annual Report (2 months) and understates the disclosure.

questions.stem: A credit default swap (CDS) is described to a retail client as 'like buying insurance against a company defaulting.' Which statement about CDS is MOST important for an adviser to add?

options.A: A CDS is exchange-traded and margined daily like a futures contract
options.B: The CDS premium is tax-deductible in Singapore
options.C: Unlike insurance, the CDS protection buyer does not need to own the underlying bond, which means CDS can be used as a speculative instrument to bet on credit deterioration without holding the reference asset
options.D: CDS premiums are guaranteed by the MAS

questions.explanation: The most important additional disclosure is that unlike insurance, a CDS buyer does not need to own the underlying credit instrument. This is what transformed CDS from a hedging tool into a speculative one: investors can take a view on credit quality without holding any of the issuer's debt. This distinction drove the global CDS market's explosive growth and its role in the 2008 financial crisis. CDS are OTC contracts, so the exchange-traded, daily-margined description is incorrect.

questions.stem: Under the MAS Fair Dealing Guidelines, Outcome 2 is the key outcome for advisers recommending structured products. What does it state, and what does it require of an adviser recommending a structured ILP to Mdm Kwan, age 67, who wants capital safety above all?

options.A: Outcome 2 relates to transparent pricing; it requires the adviser to disclose all fees upfront
options.B: Outcome 2 requires advisers to recommend only the highest-return product available
options.C: Outcome 2 requires advisers to train staff on product knowledge only
options.D: Outcome 2 states that products and services recommended are suitable for the customer; for Mdm Kwan this means the adviser must confirm the structured ILP's risk and liquidity profile match her capital-safety objective before recommending it, including whether any capital protection applies only at maturity

questions.explanation: Fair Dealing Outcome 2 is: products and services recommended are suitable for the customer. Applied to Mdm Kwan, suitability requires the adviser to verify that the product's risk level, liquidity terms, and capital-protection conditions match her primary objective of capital safety. If the ILP offers capital protection only at maturity after many years, and Mdm Kwan may need the funds before then, the recommendation fails the suitability test under Outcome 2.

questions.stem: A discount certificate is best described as a product that:

options.A: guarantees the return of capital plus a minimum coupon at maturity
options.B: mirrors the underlying one-for-one with no cap and no discount
options.C: lets the investor buy exposure to the underlying below its market price, in exchange for capping the upside at a strike level
options.D: pays an enhanced coupon in exchange for the investor writing a put option on the underlying

questions.explanation: A discount certificate is built from two options so the investor gains exposure at a discount to the market price, trading away the gains above the cap-strike. It carries no capital guarantee, and the enhanced-coupon-for-written-put design describes a reverse convertible instead.

questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST appropriate as a suitability-based recommendation for Mr Chong, age 59, who is 1 year from retirement, has a conservative risk appetite, and needs full liquidity within 18 months?

options.A: A 12-month structured deposit with a guaranteed minimum return and no early-exit penalties
options.B: A money market fund accessible daily with no lock-up
options.C: A 5-year structured ILP with capital protection only at maturity and a 5% front-end charge
options.D: A 12-month fixed deposit at a bank covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme

questions.explanation: A 5-year structured ILP is the least appropriate because: the maturity in year 5 far exceeds Mr Chong's 18-month liquidity need, capital protection arrives only at maturity making early exit loss-prone, the 5% front-end charge plus annual fund charges means the fund must earn substantially just to break even, and his conservative risk appetite clashes with a long lock-up. All other options match his horizon and risk profile. This is the horizon mismatch failure the study text repeatedly warns against.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence of margin payments on a futures position?

options.A: Maintenance margin opens the position, and initial margin is the daily top-up
options.B: Variation margin opens the position, and maintenance margin is paid at expiry
options.C: Initial margin is required only for short positions; long positions are margin-free
options.D: Initial margin opens the position; when equity falls to the maintenance margin, a margin call requires a variation margin top-up

questions.explanation: Initial margin is deposited to open the position. Daily mark-to-market then adjusts the account, and when equity falls to the maintenance level the broker issues a margin call, which the investor meets by paying variation margin. Long and short futures positions are both margined.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the marketing and distribution costs of an ILP sub-fund is correct?

options.A: Marketing costs may be charged to the sub-fund if disclosed in the Product Highlights Sheet
options.B: Marketing costs may be charged to the sub-fund as long as they do not exceed 0.5% of NAV per year
options.C: Marketing costs may be charged to the sub-fund if the policy owner gives written consent
options.D: Marketing and distribution costs must NOT be charged to the ILP sub-fund under any circumstances, because doing so would unfairly erode the existing policy owners' units

questions.explanation: The MAS rules are clear: marketing and promotional expenses may not be charged to the sub-fund. The cost is borne by the insurer separately. Charging it to the fund would reduce the NAV for all existing policy owners who had nothing to do with the marketing campaign for new investors. None of the exceptions listed in options A, B and C exist in the rules.

questions.stem: Mdm Seah, age 44, is considering two products: (X) a 5-year structured note linked to an equity basket with 100% capital protection at maturity issued by a BBB-rated bank, and (Y) a structured fund linked to the same equity basket. She says, 'Product X is safe because the bank guarantees my capital.' Which is the most accurate adviser response?

options.A: Product X does protect capital at maturity provided the issuing bank does not default; however, the protection is only as strong as the BBB-rated bank's creditworthiness, and if she exits before maturity she receives a mark-to-market value that may be below her investment
options.B: Product X is completely risk-free because it has the bank's guarantee
options.C: Product Y is safer because structured funds are guaranteed by the MAS
options.D: Product X is risk-free and Product Y carries unlimited downside risk

questions.explanation: Capital protection in a structured note is delivered by the fixed-income component; the bank is the obligor. If the bank defaults, investors are unsecured creditors and may not recover their capital. A BBB rating is investment grade but not risk-free. Furthermore, protection applies only at maturity; early exit means a mark-to-market value. The study text states: protection is only as good as the party providing it. Structured funds are not guaranteed by MAS.

questions.stem: A chooser option is best described as:

options.A: An option whose payoff is based on the highest price the underlying reached during the option's life
options.B: An option where the investor decides by a specified choice date whether the option will function as a call or a put
options.C: An option that can be exercised only on pre-set dates before expiry
options.D: An option that pays a fixed cash sum if it expires in the money

questions.explanation: A chooser option (or 'you-choose' option) lets the holder choose whether it will be a call or a put by a specified date during the option's life. This is different from a lookback option (highest price during the life), a Bermuda option (pre-set exercise dates), or a binary/digital option (fixed cash payout). Chooser options are listed among the exotic option types in Chapter 3 of the study text.

questions.stem: Mr Vijay, age 51, holds S$120,000 in a 5-year portfolio bond he purchased 2 years ago. He is considering surrendering it because of underperformance. The surrender charge is 4% in year 2. The current portfolio value is S$114,000 (net of all fund charges). Excluding the surrender charge he also faces a S$100 valuation statement charge. What are the total surrender costs and what is his net exit value?

options.A: Surrender charge = S$4,560; net exit = S$109,440 - S$4,560 - S$100 = S$104,780
options.B: Surrender charge = S$4,800; net exit = S$109,100
options.C: Surrender charge = S$4,560; net exit = S$109,440
options.D: Surrender charge = S$4,560; net exit = S$109,440 minus S$100 = S$109,340

questions.explanation: Surrender charge = 4% x S$114,000 = S$4,560. Post-surrender value = S$114,000 - S$4,560 = S$109,440. Valuation statement charge = S$100. Net exit proceeds = S$109,440 - S$100 = S$109,340. Stopping at S$109,440 omits the valuation charge, S$4,800 charges 4% on the original S$120,000 instead of the current value, and deducting the S$4,560 a second time double-counts the surrender charge. Surrender charges on a portfolio bond apply to the current portfolio value, not the original investment.

questions.stem: In the Superior Income Plan (SIP) case study, what is the role of the six reference stocks?

options.A: They serve only as a benchmark that sets the payout and the early-redemption trigger; the premium is not invested in them
options.B: The single premium is invested equally across the six stocks
options.C: They are collateral pledged by XYZ Bank to secure its guarantee
options.D: Dividends from the six stocks fund the guaranteed 4% annual payout

questions.explanation: The SIP premium goes into the ILP sub-fund's holdings, not the six stocks. The stocks are a reference basket: the number of days all six stay at or above 92% of their starting price drives the non-guaranteed payout, and all six reaching 108% or above triggers early redemption.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes how the frequency of automatic portfolio rebalancing in a portfolio bond can be set?

options.A: Only annually, to minimise transaction costs
options.B: Daily or weekly, to capture short-term movements
options.D: Monthly, quarterly, half-yearly, or annually, at the policy owner's election

questions.explanation: Portfolio rebalancing in a portfolio bond can be set to run automatically at monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or annual intervals. The study text lists all four frequencies explicitly. The 'only annually' option understates the flexibility. Daily or weekly are not listed options in the study text and would generate excessive transaction costs.

questions.stem: Mdm Rashidah, age 39, receives a Product Highlights Sheet for a structured ILP sub-fund. She notices it shows two rates of return: 1.85% and 3.35%. She asks her adviser whether these are the fund's predicted returns. The adviser's correct response is:

options.A: These are two hypothetical illustration rates required by regulation; they show the range of possible outcomes under different scenarios but the insurer is expressly forbidden from predicting actual performance
options.B: These are the guaranteed minimum and maximum returns under the policy
options.C: These are MAS-mandated fixed returns that the fund will definitely achieve
options.D: These are the bid and offer prices expressed as annual percentages

questions.explanation: The Product Highlights Sheet must show two hypothetical return rates to demonstrate the uncertainty of potential returns. The insurer shall not predict actual future performance. The rates shown (1.85% and 3.35% in the study text's sample benefit illustration) are illustrative assumptions, not guarantees or predictions. The 'guaranteed minimum and maximum' option is the exact misconception this disclosure requirement is designed to prevent.

questions.stem: Under forward pricing in an ILP, why might the number of units actually received differ from what the policy owner calculated at the time of the subscription request?

options.A: Because the insurer has the right to change the NAV retroactively
options.B: Because the fund manager invoices the policy owner separately for performance fees
options.C: Because units are dealt at the NEXT computed NAV after the dealing deadline, which is not known at the moment of the subscription request, so any price movement between the request and the next valuation changes the number of units allocated
options.D: Because the death benefit calculation adjusts the number of units at inception

questions.explanation: Forward pricing means the subscription is executed at the next computed NAV after the dealing deadline, not at the price visible when the order is placed. If the NAV rises between the request and the next valuation point, fewer units are allocated; if it falls, more are allocated. This is the mechanism described in the study text: you do not know the exact price at the moment you transact. Historic pricing (using the last known NAV) would eliminate this uncertainty but is not the standard for ILPs.

questions.stem: Mr Bala, age 47, holds a whole-life participating policy for protection. He also wants to grow his savings and is looking at structured products. His adviser notes that the Choice Fund (Case 2) is a closed-ended fund with a fixed maturity date and limited liquidity. Which risk of the Choice Fund should the adviser MOST prominently flag given the fund's characteristics described in the case study?

options.A: That the Choice Fund is covered by the DIS and therefore low risk
options.B: That the Choice Fund has unlimited liquidity because it is an open-ended fund
options.C: That the fund has no performance benchmark and no fixed asset allocation, making market risk hard to assess; combined with a small NAV of S$6.8 million heavily concentrated in OTC fixed income, liquidity risk is elevated and the fund may be unable to meet high withdrawal requests
options.D: That the Choice Fund offers a guaranteed Secure Price equal to the highest historical NAV

questions.explanation: The Choice Fund case study identifies four specific risks: non-guaranteed Secure Price (not a floor), market risk (NAV already fell ~7% since inception), liquidity risk (only S$6.8 million NAV, heavily in OTC fixed income, may not meet large withdrawals), and derivatives risk (relies on an external Golden Derivative Fund). The adviser should prominently flag the liquidity risk and the absence of a performance benchmark, which makes it hard to assess the market risk the client is taking on. The Secure Price is explicitly non-guaranteed.

questions.stem: An adviser reviews the semi-annual report of an ILP sub-fund and notes the following performance data: 1 year: fund +2.7%, benchmark +13.3%; 3 years: fund +29.4%, benchmark +35.9%; 5 years: fund +8.5%, benchmark +12.2%; 10 years: fund +15.2%, benchmark +14.1%; since inception: fund +8.7%, benchmark +7.2%. The adviser tells the client, 'This fund has a strong track record as it has beaten its benchmark.' Which statement best describes the problem with this advice?

options.A: There is no problem; citing since-inception and 10-year outperformance is sufficient
options.B: The adviser has selectively cited only the periods where the fund outperformed (10 years and since inception) while omitting the 1-year, 3-year and 5-year periods where the fund underperformed by 10.6, 6.5 and 3.7 percentage points respectively; presenting only favourable data is misleading
options.C: The problem is that the fund's benchmark is not the STI and therefore the comparison is invalid
options.D: There is no problem as long as past performance warnings are included in the brochure

questions.explanation: The fund has underperformed the benchmark in every recent measurement window: 1-year by 10.6 points, 3-year by 6.5 points, 5-year by 3.7 points. Outperformance only appears in the 10-year and since-inception periods, which capture older data. An adviser who quotes only the outperforming periods is cherry-picking. The study text explicitly makes this point: a representative who quotes only the since-inception figure is presenting a fund that has lost ground against its benchmark in every recent window. This violates the fair dealing obligation to present complete, balanced information.
